Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. Le Droit of May 6, 1953, reports the following facts in an article entitled:
Mr. Humphrys' attitude shocks many people
"You can see the minister, and your Pope if you want to". That is what Mr. F. A. Humphrys, chief of the taxation division at the income tax district office and creator of the notorious form bearing his name, replied to a French-speaking taxpayer who went to see him to obtain additional information about her income tax return.
Le Droit has made a thorough investigation among people who obtained interviews with Mr. Humphrys and others who were not able to see him. In each case Mr. Humphrys' words show his aversion to everything Catholic and French-Canadian.
"You can see the minister, and your Pope if you want to." Those are Mr. Humphrys' exact words to a female civil servant who went to see him in his office.
Mr. Chairman, in the name of all French-Canadian taxpayers in this country I wish to protest personally against the anti-national and shameful conduct of a civil servant and I ask that the government dismiss this official of the income tax division.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

May I
direct a question to the Minister of National Defence? Were security regulations cleared with the Department of National Defence before the publication by mines and technical surveys in the Canada Air Pilot, of information relating to R.C.A.F. stations in northern Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) also gave me notice of a similar question. I shall try to answer his question also, although it was couched a little differently from that of the hon. member for Nanaimo.
You cannot keep air strips secret, and there is no effort made to do so. The report which gives rise to this question was headed "secret air charts on sale in Ottawa", and that is not correct. There are no secret air charts on sale in Ottawa. The department of government concerned with civil aviation prepares charts of all airfields, service and civilian, for the use of civilian and service pilots. This is done in every free country, subject to a very few exceptions, none of which comes to my mind.
What is classified and what we endeavour to keep secret is the purpose for which certain airfields may be used, and the fact that they fit into a system. Now, both of these factors are disclosed and dealt with in the article in the Gazette, which gives rise to these questions. We try to keep that information confidential. We try to avoid giving the information which would disclose a system or the purpose of an airfield. Obviously, the location of all air strips is well known, and their location and characteristics should be knowr to facilitate civil aviation, emergency landings and the like. There has been no breach of security whatever.

May I ask a supplementary question? In view of the information which is contained in Canada Air Pilot concerning the length of these runways, would the minister consider either restricting the sale of the publication or taking some other step to prevent that information from falling into unauthorized hands? According to the minister's own statement regarding these air strips, they could be used by the enemy as steppingstones from which to leapfrog towards settled areas.
4904	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No, sir, I would not do that.
It is the practice, under the international civil aviation agreement, that charts are made up giving a list of specified information. These charts are available to air pilots, and we follow the same practice as the United States, the United Kingdom, France and all the other countries in the agreement. We could not make an exception.

speechtext: 79. Departmental administration and payments to Canadian Commercial Corporation and other corporate agencies for services provided in connection with defence purchasing and production, $6,710,933.

Mr. Chairman, yesterday
evening we heard an extremely interesting statement from the minister regarding the
[Mr. Pearkes.l

care which the department and the government takes to see that the people of Canada receive full value for their money. Just by way perhaps of an aside, I should like to refer to an interjection made by the minister in the course of the speech of my friend the hon. member for Melfort at the time when he was discussing the army camp at Penhold. It appears that perhaps our strictures of the government for its extravagance and wasteful habits have borne some fruit because in Hansard we find this most interesting statement by the minister recorded at page 4887 wherein he says:
I did my best to get the committee to go to Penhold. I offered to provide a government plane and pay for the entertainment out of my own pocket.
First, I think we should express appreciation of that generous gesture from the minister; and second, I think we should say that we are glad to see that he was trying to save the government some money. However, I also want to point this out to him since he appears to have been a little bit hurt by the fact that his invitation was not accepted. He says:
It seems to me that the committee ought to have done me the courtesy of going and looking at this so-called monstrosity . . .
I can tell him that as far as I am concerned-and this applies to all the members of the committee to whom I have been able to speak between last night and this morning-no notification was received of any such invitation. Had we received notification, I can assure the minister that we certainly would have done him the courtesy of a reply, although I doubt greatly whether we would have accepted it. With the feeling of cordiality and so on which this provision of entertainment no doubt would engender, I do not know whether any one of us would feel free, after having accepted the minister's hospitality, to continue criticizing the camp; and since we undoubtedly would have found subjects for criticism there, we would have been placed in a most embarrassing situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not sense
enough to be embarrassed.

The minister is prone to judge others by himself. I suggest that it is a practice from which he should desist.
It is a fact, of course, that at Penhold- as was pointed out by the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Wetaskiwin last night-there is a great deal to criticize. But before coming to specific subjects of criticism, I should like to deal with some of the more general statements which the minister made in the course of his remarks

here last night and in the course of his previous statements both inside and outside of the house as to the fact-according to him-that the government is not guilty of waste, extravagance or inefficiency in so far as-and I will confine it in this case-his own department is concerned.
The minister has on other occasions drawn attention to the fact that he has spent more of the taxpayers' money than has any other minister and that he therefore is a man highly qualified to talk about the subject of spending. With that statement no one would disagree. But the question arises whether the minister knows as much about saving. He has told us they exercised great care in this program of stockpiling. Not long ago, in a broadcast on "The Nation's Business", on Tuesday, April 7, the minister told us that the government exercises great care in eliminating all expenditures that are not essential. Then toward the close of his broadcast he said:
Furthermore, no one has proven waste or extravagance or inefficiency related to a single expenditure made during that long period.
I wonder whether the minister can give us an adequate explanation of some of the activities of his own department in that connection, when we find this situation, for instance. When attention was called to the fact that the department has purchased over one million neckties at a cost of over $300,000 and attention was drawn to that matter in the house, the Prime Minister, as reported at page 39 of Hansard of November 24, 1952, made the statement:
I do not know why over a million neckties were required: it may very well be that that was a mistake.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that that is hardly consonant with the assertion by the Minister of Defence Production that the greatest care is exercised in the course of his stockpiling program to ensure that there is no waste or extravagance. Many other examples could be given.
I want to give an example dealing with a different type of expenditure, namely the expenditure connected with aircraft production. I should make it clear that my question here-and I will put it in the form of a question-is based on an article appearing in Maclean's magazine of February 1, 1953, which was prefaced with this opening paragraph found at page 7 of that issue:
Maclean's was well along with an investigation of its own into the broad field of defence expenditures when the Currie report cast a new and foreboding shadow across an already turbid scene . . . Maclean's doesn't profess to have anything approaching a complete and final answer to the question: are we getting our money's worth in
Supply-Defence Production
defence? But during its own inquiries this magazine has amassed a great deal of evidence, some of it reassuring, some of it dismaying.
Then, dealing with a specific subject about which I have made inquiries, the magazine at page 50 also refers to neckties, about which, as I have just said, the Prime Minister admits that they have no adequate explanation and that it may very well have been a mistake.
Then it goes on to deal with the situation with respect to the CF-100 as follows:
Defence production ordered a supply of United States electronic apparatus to be installed in the CF-lOO's nose for all weather fighting. The CF-100's airframe was designed especially for this apparatus when only the electronic equipment's weight and dimensions were known. For the CF-lOO's speed, the electronic gear has to have an effective range of two miles.
After Avro's aero dynamicists had worked for months on the CF-lOO's design an R.C.A.F. pilot was sent to the southern United States to test the electronic equipment on order there and found that it had a reliable range of about a quarter of a mile. When another satisfactory electronic aimer and range finder was obtained, it was either a different weight or different size which threw all the earlier aerodynamic calculations into a muddle. The CF-100 airframe had to be largely redesigned.
Whatever happened, R.C.A.F. men are said to have commented privately that the CF-100 program is at least a year behind what they had hoped for when the first prototype was delivered.
I have pointed out, Mr. Chairman, that this is a statement contained in a magazine article, but a responsible magazine, prefaced by the introductory paragraph that the magazine had done a good deal of independent research and inquiry before the author wrote and the magazine put out the article. I have no personal knowledge of whether the facts are correct, but in the absence of an explanation or a denial we are entitled to rely upon the accuracy of these statements. If they are correct, then it certainly seems to me there is evidence of gross carelessness in the spending of the people's money.
While everyone must be prepared to make allowances for engineering and design difficulties between the drawing board and eventual production, and particularly perhaps to make allowances for modifications or improvements in design of electronic equipment on which no charge of inefficiency could be based, yet if delays or increased expenditure resulted from these factors, that is, in any one of these examples it then appears to me to be an example of great carelessness that a particular type of equipment was ordered, the weight was known, the airframe was designed to accommodate that particular type of equipment, and all this was done without any test of the equipment which would have established whether or not it was suitable for the purpose for
4906	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production which it was to be installed in the machine. And when the test was finally made, after the design had been perfected to accommodate that particular piece of equipment, it was found that it was not suitable for the purpose for which it was to be installed.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Just to straighten my hon.
friend out, I may say there was no electronic equipment of that kind in existence in February of this year. It is not fully developed as yet. The statement is entirely erroneous. I may say that the research done by Maclean's magazine was done largely in the office of defence production.

If the research was done largely in the office of defence production, then it seems strange to me. What the minister is saying either does not reflect what they found there, or they did find these things.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I will admit that I would rather take the views of a cub reporter than my hon. friend's, but they are both wrong in that particular.

The minister in his usual manner has dismissed this statement in Maclean's as completely erroneous. If the minister says it is erroneous, with all the knowledge of his experts that he has behind him, we have to accept that explanation. In the course of questioning in the committee this is a matter which should be followed up, because it seems to me, in the answers to the questions which I have received earlier, reference has certainly been made to electronic gun aimers and apparatus of that type. Therefore we do not know whether the minister's answer is a complete and effective rebuttal of the statements which are contained in the magazine.
He has been wrong before.

Another general subject which I should like to deal with is the delays which we have encountered in the obtaining of information which it is desirable to obtain, firstly, as an adequate and complete knowledge of all aspects of the Department of Defence Production; and secondly, in order to discuss certain matters on the items of the department now before us.
I could give many examples, Mr. Chairman, of these delays, but I have only to refer you and the committee to the first two questions on today's order paper. Question number 1 in my name has been on the order paper since February 25. It asks:
What are the particulars of the item for machine tools, equipment and installation, et cetera, sold to George T. Davie & Sons Limited, for $116,000, as surplus crown assets as shown at page 20 of the


Crown Assets Disposal Corporation report for 1950-51?
2.	What was the original cost of acquisition and installation of these items and when were they acquired and installed?
3.	Were tenders invited for the purchase of these items?
This question has been on the order paper for two and a half months without being answered. I can see no satisfactory reason why it should be left that long without being answered. It is not a minor matter, Mr. Chairman. You will recall that the firm of George T. Davie & Sons Limited is the firm which built ships for the Ming Sung company on which the people of Canada are still paying under the guarantee given to the banks, and to which firm $450,000 of an advance was written off, and to which firm subsequently $449,000 has been paid by way of the fixed fee portion of their subsequent shipbuilding contracts with the government. It is the firm which has received $1 million by way of gift through write-off or by way of fixed fee payments on contracts.
According to the information contained in the Crown Assets Disposal Corporation's report, that firm has apparently purchased certain machine tools, equipment and installations for the sum of $116,000. These machine tools, and so on, were formerly the property of the government. It is most essential that the committee and the country should have the information asked for in that question; that is:
What was the original cost of acquisition and installation of these items and when were they acquired and installed?
What was the cost of these items which the company has subsequently been allowed to purchase for the sum of $116,000? It is essential that we should know whether or not tenders were invited for the purchase of these items.
This is another example of delays in providing necessary information. I refer you to question number 2 on today's order paper which has been there since March 3, which was today passed as an order for return. Mr. Chairman, we have had so many unfortunate experiences with orders for returns in this house that I think I can predict now what will be the fate of this particular order, and I think I can predict now that that order will not be brought down during this session. If it is, I shall be glad to apologize for having suggested that it might not be down during this session. But it is not within my understanding as to why a question which has been on the order paper for two months and four days-from March 3 to May 7-should now, within four or five days probably of the end of the session, be passed as an order

for return. If it was necessary to have it made an order for return, why was that not made an order for return within a week or ten days of the day it appeared on the order paper?
I would point out that the information asked for in this question is important to the house and country, because it is information as to the total paid out on the fixed or percentage fee portion of all defence and defence production contracts since the outbreak of war in Korea. I suggest this is a subject of importance, and that it would be most opportune to have that information before us at a time when we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Defence Production, which lets the contracts.
In addition to these examples of delay and refusal of information, there are many others. There are cases when there have not merely been delays in action, but there have been definite refusals by ministers concerned. They consort very ill with the other statements made by the Minister of Defence Production in an attempt to persuade the people of Canada that the government, and his department, give all the information they are ever asked for.

And this was made in the course of a radio speech in which can be found a number of other equally amazing statements.
Any member of parliament can obtain full information about any expenditure of public moneys simply by asking for that information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: And that is true.

Well, Mr. Chairman, that last remark by the Minister of National Revenue is a joke. It is one of the most amazing things I have ever heard in this House of Commons for a long time.
Of course there are various ways of making sure that members do not get information. In addition to the examples to which I have referred, namely the MacNab report, and the information sought by the hon. member for Brandon concerning recommendations regarding auxiliary services, there is a method,

Supply-Defence Production which has been followed in the past on other occasions, of letting a question remain on the order paper until the end of the session, when it dies, or letting it stand over for two months and then passing it as an order for return.
I recall another occasion when early in the session of 1950 I asked for information with respect to government contracts. My question was passed as an order for return, and was finally brought down in November of 1951. There are ways of making sure that members do not get information. And I have given only a few of the many examples to which reference might be made.
Then, I should like to come to some specific criticism of the activities of the department, with special reference to what I regard as a tendency toward unsound methods of contracting. We heard last night from the hon. member for Wetaskiwin a very forceful and clear statement of the sort of thing that went on at Penhold, where the contractor who made the lowest tender and was awarded the contract, subsequently by way of additional orders and variations in the contract was awarded a considerable increase in the amount he received. Yet at the same time he was unable to live up to the terms of his tender. While he was in arrears in the matter of construction and of delivery dates he was awarded another large government contract for another job not many miles away from the site at Penhold.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: For which he was also the low tenderer.

Yes, for which he was also the low tenderer. But we are told by one minister that when contractors have records of inability to meet delivery dates, and the like, the department sometimes makes pretty rigid and careful inquiries as to whether such a contractor is in fact qualified as a contractor, even though he may submit the lowest tender.
But I am not going to base too much criticism on that point, because I believe in the tender system. I believe it is a sound system, provided it is adequately-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Wonderful.

Well, the minister says "wonderful". It is a pity he does not follow it. It is a pity his department does not show more affection for the tender system, instead of showing such an inclination to award contracts without tenders and on a fixed or percentage fee basis. We saw several examples of this in the committee on defence expenditure. I am thinking particularly of the cases at Churchill and Goose

Bay where the attitude of the officials in the minister's department, which I suppose would reflect his own attitude, was in complete defence of the cost-plus system of contracting.
In the case of Goose Bay there was a contract involving several millions of dollars awarded to one firm, without tender, and on a cost-plus-fee basis. And the defence given was, "Well, that contractor had a certain amount of equipment up there. It is a long way and involves a long haul. The construction season is short and we felt therefore that it was most economical to award him the contract without tender, and on a cost plus fixed fee basis."
The same holds true of Churchill where the Foundation Company of Canada has contracts which, according to the public accounts for 1952 at pages N-29 and N-30, totalled $12,755,460.82, and all of them on a cost plus fixed fee basis. The fee element in the contracts for that one company, Foundation Company of Canada Limited, amount to $516,634 for the one year covered in this public accounts report. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that that is not small potatoes. Over half a million dollars in fees in connection with contracts awarded to the one company in one year's public accounts.
The defence of that method of awarding contracts is that Churchill is a remote region and that this company is up there doing work and when more work is required to be done it is logical to award the contract to that company without asking for tenders, without asking any other company whether it would be interested in doing the work and would accept a lower fee portion for its work, whether it would be able to do it cheaper; without any investigation as to whether any other company could do it cheaper. That is the evidence given by the officials of the department in connection with contracts at Goose Bay.
If that principle is applied you can see the situation you get into. These are permanent installations, particularly at Churchill. It is conceivable that it may be necessary to spend upwards of $50 million there before we are through. Does that mean that the Foundation Company of Canada, just because it did the first work, is going to get all the contracts there? That surely is not a sound system. That is absurd. But that is the principle which was laid down and outlined to us in the defence expenditure committee.
I suggest to you that that is a complete negation of the system under which contracts should be awarded, that is on the basis that the most work will be produced for the least money. According to the

testimony given, there were no consultations even with other companies as to whether they could do it for less, as to whether they would be interested in doing the work, as to whether they would accept a lower percentage fee for doing it. No; the company that was already on the spot was to be awarded the contract without any further investigation or consultation, merely because it happened to be in there first.
That is not very reassuring in the face of a statement made to the Canadian industrial preparedness association on October 26, 1952-and this is the association which was praised by the minister last night. In its bulletin of November 1 this appears:
A. O. Matthews, financial adviser of the Department of Defence Production, replied to the effect that the cost-plus type of contract was regarded as the least desirable sort.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Read it all.

All right, I will read it all.
There are some cases where, without any basis of previous cost experience, the cost-plus contract is the only alternative. The current thinking in the department runs first toward the competitive type of contract by tender. Secondly, an attempt is made to work out a contract for first types by negotiation. Where cost-plus is the initial basis for a contract, every endeavour is made to think in terms of target prices. Here is an incentive for management to save funds and, at the same time, to make some profit. The principle of ''cost-plus" is looked on as an invitation to extravagance, and the thinking today is very much in terms of target prices.
Yet we are told that in connection with that contract at Goose Bay there were no consultations with other companies, that the company on the spot was awarded the contract on a cost-plus basis. They did not call for tenders. They did not consider calling for tenders. The same situation appears to have prevailed at Churchill where one company now has over $12 million worth of contracts on which it has earned percentage fees of over $516,000 in the one year under review in the last public accounts report.
If the principle laid down by the department and the minister is to foe followed in connection with construction which may eventually cost $50 million, this same company will get all the contracts on the same cost-plus basis. I would point out that this principle of awarding contracts without tenders and on a cost-plus basis is not new to this department; it is not something which has developed just after Korea. It has been part of their thinking for at least three years.
In sessional paper 169A of November 16, 1951, it is shown that Canadian Commercial Corporation, the predecessor of one of the agencies under the present department, 68108-310i
Supply-Defence Production awarded the following contracts for the Department of National Defence without calling for tenders:	In 1947, 7 contracts without
tenders and 2 on a fixed fee basis; in 1948, 18 contracts without tenders and 7 on a fee basis; in 1949, 22 contracts without tenders and 17 on a fee basis. The totals for the three years were 47 contracts without tenders and 26 on a fee basis. The total value for the three years was $25,949,684.21 and the total fees earned were $830,151. Therefore it is apparent that this principle of cost-plus contracts, to the rejection of the tender system, is not new with the Department of Defence Production.
There are other objections which can be taken to this method of contracting or doing business by the department, and I refer to the disposal of government assets. I have one example in mind, but there are others, concerning the sale of firearms. A question was asked regarding the proceeds from the sale of revolvers and whether tenders had been called for their purchase. The information given was that bids were solicited from the trade, but I am advised that there were firms in the firearms and sporting goods business, other than the one to which they were eventually sold, who were not asked to bid on this particular lot of revolvers.
I am told by them that the price which they would have been prepared to pay for this equipment was about 75 per cent higher, according to their best estimate, than the unit price at which they were eventually sold. It appears that not only in connection with the awarding of contracts for construction and the payment out of public funds does this department follow principles and systems which do not get the best value for our money, but also that in the disposal of crown assets, in at least one case and I should judge in numbers of cases, systems and principles are followed which do not result in the receipt by the people of Canada of the maximum amount they should get for the items disposed of.

If the hon. member would
care to give us the name of the firm to which he is referring I shall be glad to look into it. The question of the disposal of firearms and that sort of thing is covered by certain regulations which have to be adhered to. It may be that this particular firm did not meet those requirements. I shall be pleased to look into it and let the hon. member know, if he will give us the name.

I am told that I am free to
use the name, but I do not propose to give it in the house. I shall let the hon. member know so that inquiries can be made. I am

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member answered his own question. We have reciprocal agreements with the disposal agency in the United States that neither will sell goods for disposal in the other country without prior agreement. If he intended to sell his goods in the United States he would be automatically barred from buying them from our disposal agency under usual circumstances.

The minister has not got the point. These goods were disposed of to a Canadian company which resold them in the United States. That is the situation. When inquiries were made by the company which objected to not having been asked to tender they were told that there was only a limited number of tenders called because the department only called from firms which had outlets or contacts in the United States. My information was that the contractor of whom I speak was perfectly prepared to dispose of the goods on the same basis-he could have disposed of them in the United States-but he was not given an opportunity to tender.
Mr. Chairman, those are the sort of examples which I have in mind and which, I suggest, raise very serious doubts about whether or not the people of Canada are getting value in connection with money which is spent for purchases, on their behalf, of new equipment and items or with respect to disposal of items for which they have previously paid through their tax money. Those matters, I suggest to you, sir, very definitely refute the passage in the majority report of the committee on defence expenditure where they say:
The construction program in the face of a number of difficulties has been- well conceived and carefully supervised and the public has received good value for its money.
Those words, so unjustified on the basis of the evidence we received before the committee, reflect the wishful thinking of the government majority in the house. I can assure you, sir, and the minister, and the chairman of the defence expenditure committee, that they will not for one moment hoodwink the public.
[Mr. Fulton.)

Mr. Chairman, I was not a
member of the defence expenditure committee but I did keep in very close touch with what was going on in the committee by frequent conferences with the member who represented our group in the committee, and also by way of the daily reports of the evidence which was taken. I have read the committee's report which was brought into this house and I want to say now, Mr. Chairman, that I am convinced that the committee's report is a complete whitewash of a host of what can only be described as amazing and pretty bleak facts that were brought out in the course of the examination of witnesses before the committee.
The committee's work was in some respects valuable; one has to admit that. I am glad that it was. But it was far from complete work and in no way can it be said to have been thorough work. I am perfectly sure that the government knew beforehand that work in that committee could not possibly be thorough, and I am quite sure they knew the report that would be brought down would in no way reflect on the government's department-regardless of what was brought out in the committee. We all knew that it could not be such a reflection and that is why we, in this corner of the house, proposed a full judicial inquiry into the whole of the activities of the Department of National Defence with particular emphasis on the defence construction end. We got little support for that idea so we went along with the demand that Mr. Currie be commissioned to finish the job that he had started and, of course, to extend it over the whole of Canada.
Well, here we are now with the report brought to us in the final days of the session, a report of the Liberal majority on its own departmental activities. That report completely suppresses the sordid facts and details of the evidence which one reads, and which I have read, in the daily reports of the committee's investigation. There are many pieces, I would say, of unfinished business which in the public interest ought to have been finished by the committee before this session ended. Of course, there was neither opportunity nor, I would think, inclination to finish it as it should have been finished. As a consequence, the taxpayers of Canada are taking what I am going to call an artistic shellacking. That is putting it in common terms. If we do not devise some different means and ways of protecting the taxpayers' interests they are going to continue to take a shellacking.

Last evening my colleague from Wetaski-win revealed to the house some astounding facts concerning defence construction in my own province particularly, and I would like to review briefly and to marshal together some of the more important things that he brought out-to carry the picture just a little further because I think the public will want to read it and see for themselves. 1 do so, Mr. Chairman-and I want to emphasize this-only because I feel that it is a public duty since I know those facts.
Immediately after the outbreak of war in Korea the Department of National Defence decided to renovate two of the wartime airforce stations in central and northern Alberta. Those were at Penhold and Namao. They also decided to build a new bombing range at Cold Lake with the station and airport proper at Beaver Crossing, not far from Cold Lake, in northeastern Alberta.
Here are some of the facts about the projects as they were brought out in the record of the committee's investigation:
1.	The program for renovating and expanding the Penhold base was to cost $6,340,664.
2.	The largest single contract at Penhold went to Alexander Construction company of Edmonton. That contract was awarded in May of 1951 and was for the construction of twelve buildings; but it was later extended to include some additional buildings, particularly a barracks block, supply and installation of kitchen equipment in the mess, supply of pallets and bins for the unit supply building, and the installation of the electrical distribution system.
3.	The original bid put in by Alexander Construction company was $2,640,597 but later change orders brought this amount up by $594,270

making the total $3,234,867.
4.	The contract of the Alexander Construction company required that the work be finished in nine months-that would be by February of 1952. The time was later extended to May, 1952.
5.	In the fall of 1951 the Royal Canadian Air Force requested a speed-up of the work in order to have the buildings completed by February of 1952. As a consequence, arrangements were made with the contractor for a speed-up of operations for which Alexander Construction company was paid $28,254.67 in addition to his other contractual costs. After going that far, someone representing the government cancelled the speed-up program on December 11, 1951, when it became quite clear that Alexander could not finish the job before July, 1953, at the very earliest.

6. In spite of the speed-up and of the $28,000 extra cost that the speed-up involved, at this late date, two years after the first contracts were let, the Alexander Construction company has completed and turned over to the R.C.A.F. only five of the original twelve buildings that the company contracted to build. Four are almost completed and the other eight are to be completed in April.
I have not been able to learn as yet whether or not that was done.

I might clear that up for the
hon. member. As of April 8, ten of the twelve buildings were turned over completed and occupied by the R.C.A.F.

I am glad to get that information. It seems that 25 months after the granting of the contract ten of the twelve originally planned buildings have been completed and turned over. They were supposed to have been finished within nine months. No penalty clause was to be found in the contract as an inducement to get the job done, and although protests were made that it would be in the best interests of the contractor to get the job done as quickly as possible, I want to point out that practically 25 months have passed and the buildings are not completed as yet.
7.	Shortly after the cancellation of the speed-up operation at Penhold, and during the very period when the Royal Canadian Air Force was pressing for all-out speed in getting Penhold ready for their occupancy, Alexander was given another big contract at Cold Lake for 21 buildings plus a water and sewer project, totalling $4,939,673. Now, the first contract for this project to Alexander was dated March 1, 1952. Let me emphasize once again, Mr. Chairman, that this is at the very time when Alexander was stumbling along totally unable to fulfil the contracts at Penhold within twice the time he had agreed to complete them. I ask you, could the people be blamed for thinking that Alexander was enjoying preferred treatment over other contractors, and that the possible reason for it might be that he had friends at court? I just ask that question and leave it with the people themselves to find the answer.
These feelings are intensified when you examine the evidence that was brought out in the committee by the member for Wetas-kiwin. Let us look at some of the details in connection with Penhold especially. I have already stated that after Alexander was in under the wire with a contract amounting to $2,640,597 at Penhold, that contract was jacked up to $3,234,867 by change orders amounting to $594,270.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member is casting doubt on the integrity of the departmental engineers who are handling that work. As for me, I do not know Mr. Alexander, nor have I met the gentleman. So far as I know he has not been helped through my department or otherwise. I do not know how the method he suggests could be arranged, but I can assure my hon. friend that the professional engineers who handle this work are not of the type he mentions or the type he apparently associates with. They are professional men who live up to the high ethics of their profession.

I am happy to be able to say that I do not associate with any of them. I should like to say that I am not imputing any motives or crookedness on the part of the minister. I want him to know this, that during the years I have known him I have admired him. I have never said one thing against him. I think he is a great man. He has done great things for Canada. I am going to say this, that he is tired and they have piled a lot of work on him.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Don't worry about the old man.
I want to say this, that every man in my department has just as high a standard as I have. If he does not, he is not in the department long. I think my own standards are pretty good.

I gladly accept that. I am not going to argue the point with the minister at all. I am simply saying that he has had so much to do that he would not possibly be able to know all the details. I think he wants to see that everything is done on the up and up, but let me just finish the story


and we shall let the people judge for themselves. All I am stating are the facts.
Let us take a quick look at some of these change orders that the minister was telling us about. One of them was involved in the contract for water and sewer distribution at Penhold. The original contract was for $61,981, but change orders increased it by $59,788 or by almost 100 per cent of the original contract. Well, granted that was a call for extra material and so on, I was very much interested in reading just what some of these things called "ground services" were. When I looked at some of them-well, I am no judge of the cost of installing such things as shut-off valves and so on, but the prices seem pretty lush. I shall read one or two, reference to which is found on page 527 of the evidence taken by the committee.
In answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, here is what change order No. 3 involved, and it covers the ground services to buildings. There was a provision for installing 21 additional six-inch valves and boxes at $117.54 each. This sounds like a very good price to me. Here is another item: Five four-inch valves and boxes at $86.85 each; six-inch fire hydrants, nine of them, at $343.35 each. This is the cost of the hydrant and the installation, and that is in addition to the original contract which included digging the trenches. Then there is an item for one and a half inch shutoff valves at $44.85 each. Those are just some samples of the prices. They may be all right, I do not know, but they sound fairly substantial to me.
Now, here is another change order involving the drilling of two new wells as well as the repairing already there. Now, Alexander was given a firm price contract for the two new wells at $13,257.66 each, which price included six and a quarter inch pipe and a small 8 foot by 8 foot frame pump house. According to the evidence the No. 3 well produced a satisfactory flow of water at 105 feet, yet the price paid was $13,257.66. Well No. 4 was drilled to a depth of 329 feet, and for each one of those wells Alexander got $13,257.66. Knowing something about what is involved in drilling water wells in that area, Alberta taxpayers could never be blamed for believing they had really been "rooked" when they look at this price.
Not only Alberta taxpayers; Canadian taxpayers.
I am speaking of those in that area who saw it and who complained about it. I suppose you could find ample illustrations all over Canada of similar things.
Is this all rock?

No. It is not all rock. It could not have been, as my hon. friend will see. This will answer my hon. friend's question. Then they see that Alexander was also given a contract to clean out the sand from another well that had been drilled on the base some years ago. It is easy drilling in that area. There is a great deal of sand and loam. This contract for cleaning out this well was supposed to be on a cost-plus basis but the final bill on it was $1,191.55, which is about what most farmers would have to pay for the drilling of a new well and providing their own water supply there and in many other areas in that country that I know about.
Change order No. 4 referred to the installation of the electrical distribution system at Penhold. It called for an amount of $141,000. When he was questioned about this item, the president of Defence Construction Limited said that the government did not ask for tenders on this item. Instead, they left the details in the hands of Alexander Construction company and they called for tenders. Of course they were paid a little fee of $6,285 for it. Sunley Electric Limited got the job of installation for $134,751. It is an amazing situation when the government, with its own facilities for calling for tenders and placing contracts and its own inspectors right on the job, takes Alexander Construction company into partnership and gives them the authority to let contracts for the government at a nice fat fee of $6,285 for their trouble. Again I ask: Is it any wonder that people ask what friends Alexander Construction company have at court?
I will not take the time, Mr. Chairman, to speak of the cement slabs which my colleague mentioned last night, nor any one of the great many other sordid and amazing details that were recorded in the minutes of the committee's proceedings. I think the facts which I have reviewed-and they alone without anything else-prove conclusively enough that there have been waste, loose handling of contracts and favouritism in defence construction, and that the report of the defence expenditure committee was a complete whitewash job.
There is every good reason, in my judgment, why it would be in the public interest to have yet a complete judicial-type inquiry into the whole defence department and the business particularly of defence construction everywhere in Canada. It would be most revealing, I assure you, Mr. Chairman, and
Supply-Defence Production useful to the people as a whole in this country if such firms as Alexander Construction Limited could be examined under oath on the witness stand as they should be.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, last night the hon. member for Wetaskiwin made certain statements just as I was coming into the chamber. I did not hear what he said at the time. After reading Hansard, however, I think I should just say a word or two. As reported at page 4895 of Hansard the hon. member said:
The thing that makes me feel rather strongly about this contract Is that until a few months prior to the calling for tenders the Alexander Construction Company was known as the Prudham Construction Company. It would appear from the position this company was put in that there still might be some connection.
I made a statement last night. I should like to elaborate on it at this time. I have lived in Edmonton for about 23 years. During that period I was able to build up a successful business. That was done on the basis of honesty, good public service and hard work.
I greatly resent the attempt that is being made, now that I am in public life, to discredit that reputation; and I know that a great many people in my part of the country also resent it.
As I said last night, when I was elected a member of the House of Commons I was the proprietor of a construction and building supplies company. When I was given the honour of being appointed parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Resources and Development, I realized that I no longer would be able to carry the responsibility of a heavy business and the demands of that office. I immediately made arrangements to sell my interest in the construction company. I sold my interest completely for cash. I have no interest whatever in it now. The arrangements made at that time were that the Prudham name would be dropped as soon as the affairs of the company could be wound up. That was before Korea. At that time there was no thought of any defence construction or any government contracts. The company was not engaged in government contracting. It had a very nice commercial business in the city of Edmonton and was building several large schools at the time.
Perhaps I made a mistake. Had I known that Korea was coming up, I might have thought of making a restriction-in the sale of that company-to the effect that the succeeding company should not tender on government contracts. However, that is afterthought.

Supply-Defence Production I do not know how the shares of the Alexander Construction company are held. I have never made inquiries. I have never been in the office of the Alexander Construction company except once and that was a week after I had completed the sale, when I went in to wish them well. Since that time I have kept strictly away from the company and the operations of the company.
In so far as the Alexander Construction company are concerned, here in Ottawa they had been at a disadvantage. Every member of the House of Commons, on occasion, does a certain amount of chores for his constituents, including companies. Neither I nor my office have done anything for the Alexander Construction company. They have been at a disadvantage. They have come here and have run their own errands. To the best of my knowledge and memory, Mr. Alexander has never been in my office in Ottawa. I do not know the details of the tenders. I never inquired to see how Alexander Construction company stood in relation to other contractors.
Having had a long experience in the construction business, I know something of the problems the Alexander Construction company and the other construction companies have had in this defence construction period. It is all very well to say that the contracts were let with a deadline for finishing them, but it was another thing to get the steel. I have been told that on many of these contracts the steel was not available until after the expiry date of the contract. You cannot blame the contractors for that situation nor can you blame the government. It was caused by the shortage of steel, and nobody could do anything about it but make the best of it.
I have never been at Penhold airport and I have never been at Cold Lake. I know nothing about what is going on there except what I have heard. At no time have I ever spoken to my colleague the Minister of Defence Production on behalf of Alexander Construction company and at no time has anyone on my staff interceded on their behalf.
I hope that what I have said puts some of the apparent misconceptions straight, Mr. Chairman. I think that my friends in the Social Credit party are pushing this matter just a little too far.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that some rather extended references have been made in this debate to the work of the committee on defence expenditure, particularly in relation to the evidence that 
was given before that Committee about the construction program, I might deal very briefly with the work of that committee in that field and with some of the assertions that have been made by various members who have preceded me. It is only fair to say that the speeches that have been made so far in this debate by members of the opposition, particularly of the official opposition and the Social Credit party, have amounted to attacks on the committee on defence expenditure and the work it did, and in fact on the whole system of examining matters of public interest by committees of parliament. That seems to be extraordinary when we recall the insistence with which certain members, particularly of the official opposition, request the government to set up committees of parliament for every conceivable reason and device.
When they get the committees, they then come back to parliament and complain that the committees have not done their work properly and that the members of the committees are not competent to deal with the matters that have been placed before them. That was said in the committee on defence expenditure. Several members said that; they said that they themselves were not competent to deal with these things, and they requested expert assistance.
They said they were not engineers.

We hear a lot of talk from the opposition about the government having contempt for parliament. In my experience here I have not seen anything to equal the contempt of parliament that is shown by the members of the opposition in their approach to this question of committees dealing with public business.
What I shall have to say in dealing with the facts of the evidence brought out in the committee in relation to statements which have been made in this debate will indicate not only to the committee but to the public who read the records of this house that the committee on defence expenditure did excellent work, and that it made findings which will fully justify the public in coming to the conclusion that is stated in the report, that in the field of defence construction public money has been well spent and the public has received full value for the money that has been expended, and the very large sums that have been expended, in this way.
Members of the opposition groups in the committee and by the so-called amendment to the report of the committee moved by the official opposition have made very definite and pointed insinuations that the civil servants and the members of the armed forces

who appeared to give evidence before the committee cannot be trusted and that their evidence should not be accepted. That is something to which I drew attention in the committee and protested against, and I protest against it again in this house with the utmost vehemence.
The men who appeared before the committee were sincere and honest public servants. They gave their evidence with the same care and regard for the truth and the absolute truth as if they had been under oath and appearing in a court of law. These innuendoes and suggestions, that in order to get at the facts we require some sort of independent and expert advice, are not borne out by the record of the committee. As a matter of fact, what we require, Mr. Chairman, is for the members, both of the committee and those who did not sit on the committee, to read the record of evidence and to understand it, and not to completely ignore it when they discuss the proceedings of the committee in the house, because that is what has been going on in this debate.
Some complaint was made because the committee dealt only with construction. There was the suggestion that the committee had been derelict in its duty in that regard. The fact is that in the previous session the committee on defence expenditure had gone in great detail into the question of programs of various types of armament, aircraft, and supplies of all kinds. It was the request of the opposition members that on this occasion this year we go into the very important and extensive construction program, which had been touched on only lightly in the previous committee. It was to meet the criticisms which had been made of this construction program that arrangements were made, very gladly made, by this department and the Department of National Defence, to facilitate the examination of the construction program by the committee in the most thorough way that would be possible. There were signs that members of the opposition regarded the construction program as a very fertile field for examination. They had high hopes that they would uncover waste, extravagance and scandals.
The fact is that, as the proceedings of the committee went forward, it was clear from the evidence that they were not going to find and could not find what did not exist, namely, waste, extravagance, and scandals in that program. And for that reason we began to be met with the suggestion that perhaps this examination of construction was not quite as valuable as it had looked at first, and we should get on to a variety of other subjects.
Supply-Defence Production
The committee was absolutely right, in the time at its disposal, in trying to deal as completely as it possibly could with the construction program. The method adopted by the steering committee was to invite the members of the opposition to select the particular construction projects that they wished to have examined, and the list that was drawn up was one of nominations by the members of the opposition of the projects that they believed were the very ones that should be examined and would disclose the kind of waste and extravagance that they wished to establish against the program. We were very glad to meet the members of the opposition in that regard and to deal with the very subjects that they requested. We have heard again today the hon. member for Kamloops complaining about the lack of information, and yet yesterday and at other times in this house we have heard the hon. member for York West and other hon. members complaining because they have been inundated with information; they got so much information they could not handle it.
The hon. member for York West is more correct than the hon. member for Kamloops. If there is any criticism of what was done by these departments in putting the evidence into the committee it would be that the evidence was too voluminous and gave too much detail. Some hon. members were inclined to throw up their hands and decide they could not examine all this great mass of detail.
I think I should now refer to just a few of the specific matters that have been brought out in this debate and to show that far from presenting facts, as the hon. member for Peace River has said, they have not been presenting the facts as disclosed by the evidence in the committee, but they have been actually presenting the complaints and the arguments that were made previously, and have been completely ignoring the evidence that was given to explain exactly what had happened and to show what the situations were. And it is only by completely ignoring what was placed before the committee by way of evidence that hon. members have been able to make any fist at all of making the kind of arguments they have placed before the committee in this debate.
The hon. member for Peace River, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin, the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Kamloops all dealt at some length with matters relating to contracts for the construction of buildings and other works at the air station at Penhold. One of the particular points raised by the hon. member for Peace River, following the hon. member for Wetaskiwin,

Supply-Defence Production was the innuendo that some preference had been extended to Alexander Construction Limited in connection with these contracts; and coupled with that was an innuendo against the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, with which he has dealt.

May I say that there was no innuendo with respect to the first thing mentioned by the parliamentary assistant. But I am not taking any responsibility for any innuendoes other than what I actually said. I said that definitely, in my opinion, preference had been given. There was no innuendo; it was a straight statement.
Well, if the hon. member for Peace River had examined the record of the evidence before the committee on defence expenditure-
I did.

-and if he had understood what is in that evidence, he would not have risen in his place in this debate and made that definite statement, or even the innuendo to that effect. Because he based his arguments, first of all, on the fact that the original Alexander contract had been extended by almost $600,000. He made the suggestion that there had been something that was planned by somebody as a way of making this contract more remunerative to Alexander Construction Limited.
The fact of the matter is that these contracts are let on competitive tenders, and the defence expenditure committee was informed of the number of tenders that were received in each of these cases, and the range of the bids. And there has been no suggestion that there was anything improper about that. These tenders are on the basis of a firm price, with firm prices for units of work. And it is clearly understood by everybody who tenders that, if any additional work is required under a particular contract, he will be required to do that work at the unit prices contained in his tender. That is one of the considerations, which shows that the tender of the lowest tenderer is really the lowest tender, and one which should be accepted.
The substantial increases in this main contract, as shown at pages 516 and 517 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the committee, are quite interesting. For instance change order number 2 was for erection of a 72-man extension to one of these buildings. In other words it had been found necessary by the Department of National Defence to extend the accommodation required, and that created a change order to provide the accommodation for 72 more men. Is the suggestion made that that change was known at the


time the tenders were called, and was held back in order to assist Mr. Alexander? I think that is the suggestion the hon. member has made.

May I answer the parliamentary assistant, although I do not wish to interrupt. Could he say at this time whether the people who were in charge of construction at Pen-hold did not know what they were building for, right from the beginning?
Not at all; they knew exactly what they were 'building for.
Then why did they not know that they had to have space for 72 more men?

Changes in plans do come up. And I am quite interested to see it is clear that the hon. member is trying to imply that some official of the Department of National Defence held this back in order to assist and to favour Alexander Construction Limited.
No, I deny that emphatically.

Utterly
unfair.
I deny it emphatically; and I wish the parliamentary assistant would not descend into that realm. We are trying to keep this discussion on a high level, and I think he should withdraw that statement.
Make him take that back.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think perhaps the parliamentary assistant did not understand exactly what the hon. member meant when he spoke earlier. However, I wish to tell the hon. member that at a certain moment I had thought there was in his remarks an implication to the effect that someone, somewhere, had held certain changes to be made later in order to favour the company to which he was referring. And if I understood it that way, it is possible that other hon. members did. If it is not what the hon. member for Peace River intended to say, and if he wishes to make it clear now, then the parliamentary assistant must accept his statement.

I would certainly withdraw any statement that was unfair; but I had the clear impression, as you did, Mr. Chairman, that that was what the hon. member had said; and I must say I cannot understand his argument, unless that is what he was saying. However, if he was saying something else, then I certainly accept that explanation.
Another increase in connection with this contract was concerning the installation of an electrical distribution system. That was a matter to which he referred with some special emphasis. I should tell the hon.

member that it is very normal practice in construction work to have a prime contractor call for firm price tenders for subcontracting work, and to require that the prime contractor be responsible for the manner in which the subcontractor carries out the work.
This is normal procedure, and it was the procedure followed in this instance. The prime contractor, Alexander Construction Limited, was required to call for firm price tenders. They awarded it to the lowest bidder, and they were required to oversee the way the work was done, and be themselves responsible for its proper completion. They were required to service that contract and to pay the subcontractor, and then, themselves, put in progress claims for payment from Defence Construction Limited. And it was for that kind of responsible work that they got a very modest fee for the servicing of the contract. That was done because it has been found to be the most economical and the best way to do this kind of work. Many of these subtrades have to correlate their work with the work of the prime contractor; and unless the prime contractor has some direct responsibility and authority over the subcontractor, difficulties and delays are inclined to arise. And it was for that reason that this procedure was followed in the present instance.
Does the parliamentary assistant admit that at the same time Defence Construction Limited could have had its own inspectors on the job, and could easily have done the job?

No. The system is that the prime contractor is held responsible to Defence Construction Limited for the proper performance of the work by the subcontractor. Defence Production Limited have their own inspectors on the job to oversee the whole thing and to inspect that part of it just the same as any other part.

My question was not whether it was the normal practice; what I wanted to know was whether Defence Construction Limited did not have their own inspectors on the job who should have done the same service.

They had their own inspectors on the job who inspected this part of it just the same as any other part. The interests of economy and the proper performance of the work dictated that it should be done in this way.

Does the hon. member mean to imply that when a prime contract is let it is the general practice to exclude such things as electrical wiring, plumbing and 68108-311J
Supply-Defence Production things of that nature, and then later on let them out as subcontracts?
I do not think that that question can be answered as to whether or not it is the general practice.
Mr. Chairman-

Will the hon. member permit me to answer. The evidence before the committee was that at the time the prime contract was let the proper information for the installation of electrical services was not available and they could not be included in the tenders of those who bid on the prime contract. For that reason they had to be let out to tender later.
That is a very peculiar situation in itself.

I am just assuring the hon. member that that was the situation. He may regard it as peculiar, but that is the fact. Another matter raised by the hon. member in connection with the Alexander Construction company was the delays that had been experienced and the fact that there was no penalty clause in the contract. The situation is that we are having considerable difficulty getting bids on firm price jobs, particularly in Alberta, without making it more difficult by having penalty clauses. I am informed that it is impossible to get a firm price bid on a substantial job anywhere in Canada with a penalty clause for the completion date.
The reason for that is that the many causes for delay on any job are outside the control of the contractor and they cannot foresee what might come up. With respect to the Penhold job, the evidence before the committee indicated that the causes of delay were largely outside the hands of the contractor. First of all, there was difficulty in getting labour. The fact is, as the hon. member probably knows, that contractors in Alberta have to bid against employers of labour who are engaged on large cost-plus contracts for private industry. There is a very competitive market for labour. In addition, the weather in Alberta in 1951 was exceptionally bad. I understand that it was only in August that no snow fell in the province.
Then there was a problem created by deliveries of structural and reinforcing steel over which the contractor had no control. This general problem became so serious that Defence Construction Limited had to set up a special branch to expedite deliveries of steel to various important construction projects.

Supply-Defence Production Then in connection with this particular job there were problems with respect to the location of buildings and soil conditions which involved delay. There was also the question of extra work required, and which was covered by the various change orders. That all took extra time and put forward the date of completion of the various buildings. These change orders are carefully checked and were issued only for work that was required.
The hon. member went on to say that while Alexander was having this difficulty at Pen-hold he was awarded another contract at Cold Lake. The fact is that once again firm price tenders were called for and the Alexander Construction company was the lowest tenderer.
Right there, Mr. Chairman-

I think I have been as accommodating as I could be and I think what I am going to say will answer the interjection the hon. member was going to make. If Defence Construction Limited, having received a low bid from Alexander Construction company, which is a recognized operator in the construction field in Alberta, had refused to accept it and had accepted a higher bid because of the delays at Penhold, then the Alexander Construction company, the hon. member and perhaps many other hon. members of the opposition could have come here and complained bitterly because they could have shown that the delays at Penhold were beyond the control of the Alexander Construction company. It would have been contended that it was grossly unfair to penalize them with respect to another contract because of those delays. That is the situation and if the hon. member will carefully read the evidence given before the committee he will see that that is correct.
Another matter raised by the hon. member was in connection with the water supply and the cost of drilling wells. The fact is that tenders were called for the drilling of these wells and the work was done under a subcontract by what I am informed is one of the leading firms doing this sort of work in Canada, the International Water Supply Company. Doubtless the hon. member knows that company and its reputation.
It is completely fantastic to compare the job of supplying water to this camp to the job of supplying water to a farm. The evidence before the committee was that the needs of a town of 3,000, service personnel and dependents, had to be met and the requirement was that there should be a flow of 200 gallons per minute. I am quite sure that


the hon. member cannot stand up in his place and tell me of any town in Alberta with a population of 3,000 that is obtaining its water supply from deep wells at that rate of flow at a lower cost than was paid at Penhold.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at one o'clock I was dealing with matters that had been raised in this debate particularly with regard to projects at Pen-hold and Cold Lake. In continuing with those remarks I should like to recall to the committee the speech made last evening in this debate by the hon. member for Melfort. The hon. member dealt in some detail with points similar to those with which I have been concerned regarding Penhold. He also raised the question of construction work at Churchill and the extremely high costs of construction operations at that location. As I understood the hon. member, he stated that he could understand and appreciate that construction costs at a location like Churchill might be something of the order of twice what normal construction costs would be at more normal localities. He made a comparison between a ten-room school built at Churchill costing about $500,000 and some school to which he referred as being built at Summerside.
It is not possible for anyone to deal with that comparison without knowing full details of the school to which he referred at Summerside, whether it was comparable construction, when it was built, and matters of that kind. However, Mr. Chairman, the interesting fact is that the hon. member did say that he could appreciate costs being something in the vicinity of twice as high in Churchill as in any other place.
If the hon. member will look at pages 700 and 701 of the proceedings of the defence expenditure committee he will read from the evidence of the president of Defence Construction Limited, who placed them on the record and explained them to the committee, the various reasons why residential and other construction at Churchill was more expensive. For instance, there was the necessity to provide additional insulation; expenditures to provide water, sewer and electrical service through covered passages rather than by underground services; and things of that kind. The evidence of Mr. Johnson on that point was that costs at Churchill were running approximately about twice what they would be expected to be for similar construction in say Montreal or Toronto.

That, Mr. Chairman, I think, is just about the clearest indication that the committee did worth-while work. If the hon. member for Melfort had consulted the evidence, his concern about high costs at Churchill would have been very, very substantially met; because, after all, he admitted that it should cost about twice what it would normally. The evidence is that construction at Churchill is running just about twice what the cost of normal construction would be.
The hon. member for Kamloops also dealt at some length with the operations at Pen-hold. I think he indicated that other firms were not asked to tender on the additional work being given to Alexander Construction company at that point.
No.

Well, the hon. member says he did not imply that, and he is quite correct if he did not. All those additional items were subject to tender calls, as I think the svidence clearly indicates. He did, however, criticize us for what he referred to as unsound methods of contracting, and he spoke particularly of cost-plus contracts at Goose Bay, at Churchill and at other locations. He quoted the statement made by a former financial adviser to the Department of Defence Production, and if hon. members will read the statement carefully they will see that it expressed very clearly the policy of the Department of Defence Production.
It is true that Mr. Matthews' statement was directed particularly to procurement contracts and not construction contracts. While there are substantial differences in some cases between procurement and construction contracts, I think the general principle is clear and it is the same throughout the whole field. Our main principle is to secure competitive firm price bids for every bit of work we do if it is at all possible to proceed in that manner. The success that has been achieved in following that procedure is indicated by the figures that were given in the committee and which were also given in this house prior to that time. They show that of all our construction contracts last year 2 per cent are on a cost plus fixed fee basis and that the total value of those contracts, that is outside the special security program, is only 8 per cent.
Hon. members of the opposition quite often hold up to us the example of the United Kingdom parliament and say that we should try to follow their way of doing things. It may be interesting to the committee to hear this exchange which appears in the United Kingdom Hansard for February 9, 1953, column 7, which is headed "Ministry of supply; contracts".
Supply-Defence Production
Sir W. Smithers asked the minister of supply if, in the interests of the taxpayer, he will discontinue contracts on a cost-plus basis and put all contracts out to competitive tender.

The overwhelming majority of our production contracts are placed on the basis of competitive tenders or fixed prices. Only in cases where costs cannot be reliably estimated in advance, as in research and development work, is payment made on a cost basis.
That is a statement that could equally well have been made in this house to describe the contracting methods and procedures which we have followed. I submit to the hon. member and to the committee that he is not in accordance with the facts when he says that we are following unsound methods of contracting. We are following the soundest possible method. We are getting good firm prices for the vast majority of our work, and we are doing that work with the protection of these firm prices.
Now, the hon. member also, in dealing with Churchill, stated that the public accounts disclose that one of the contractors at that location, the Foundation Company, had been paid, in the fiscal year 1952, as I understood him, fees of $500,000 for $12 million worth of work. The hon. member must be under some misapprehension as to the facts. The facts are that for work done from 1948, and in every fiscal year up to that time, the total amount of work performed by the Foundation Company amounted to $12 million. Over that whole period of time the company has been paid $500,000. This shows that the fees that they have received amount to something in the vicinity of 4 per cent for that very large volume of work. As has already been explained, the fees are based on a sliding scale and are fixed at the time the contract is signed.
The hon. member also said, as I understood him, that this work at places like Churchill was all being given to one company, and that no one else had an opportunity to participate. It was stated that those were going to be carefully inquired into. Well, the committee sat for many weeks and not one letter or charge was brought before it, not one charge of any wrongdoing or anything improper was proven or even attempted to be proven.
Take, for example, the matters brought up in this house earlier in the session concerning the construction at Namao. The undertaking was solemnly made in this house that, so far as we were concerned, Namao could be examined into and we would be delighted to have it examined into. question was put to him with regard to that matter. I think the committee can be pleased with the work that it did, in spite of the fact that the hon. gentlemen who, in its early stages, seemed to think that they had some serious matters to bring before it, did not see fit to bring them forward.

Mr. Chairman, on March 30 I put on the order paper four questions which read as follows:
1.	During the years 1950, 1951, 1952 and 1953 to date, who supplied milk to Camp Wainwright?
2.	At what price per quart was the milk supplied?
3.	Were tenders called?
4.	If so, who submitted bids and what were the prices quoted?
I may say that I tried to get information in connection with this matter when the estimates of the Department of National Defence were before the house, but on that occasion the minister referred me to the Department of Defence Production as they were the ones that let the contract. I am raising this question at this time because I understand that some of the dairymen at Wainwright have gone to considerable expense in equipping their farms and buying new stock in order to be able to supply the camp with milk. I understand that they supplied the camp for some time and that recently a contract has been awarded to an outsider at a price that is considerably higher than that at which Wainwright residents are prepared to supply it.
I placed these questions on the order paper in 'order to get the department's side of the matter before asking questions in committee. I wonder whether 1 can have that information today or sometime soon. I may say that I am asking for the information now because at three o'clock I am supposed to be in another committee, and it is rather hard to be in two places at one time.
