Yes, Mr. Chairman; we can get that information. It required an inquiry being sent out to the district purchasing office in Alberta; but I think we can bring down the return shortly, as I saw the preliminary preparation of the return just the other day.
Briefly, to assure my hon. friend may I say that, with respect to purchases of milk, we are required to call for tenders, but the tender call is submitted only to dairies that are

approved1 by the Department of National Defence from the point of view of health standards. In connection with the Wainwright contracts, there have been two or three cases where the bacteriological count has been found to be high and the contract has had to be changed to another dairy which met the specifications.
There is also the difficulty of the supply of milk in the kind of containers that the Department of National Defence requires. Up until a few years ago the Department of National Defence took all their supplies in bulk; that is in ordinary milk cans; but they have found that it is much more economical in the use of milk to get it in the modern cardboard container. We are required to ask for tenders on that basis. While the original cost of the milk in containers is somewhat higher than is the cost of milk in bulk, the actual over-all cost, they find, is less.

Mr. Chairman, I was aware of the fact that some alleged difficulty had arisen in connection with the pasteurization of milk; but I understand that in Wainwright there is an up-to-date pasteurization plant. That is my information.
In connection with the sample that was sent to Edmonton, I am informed that it was allowed to lie around the camp for some time before being sent up there. That fact would naturally have some effect upon the test when made at Edmonton. If there were some defects, I believe that, in view of the fact that there is a good pasteurization plant in the Wainwright territory, any alleged faults can be corrected. As there is a difference of 8 cents a quart, according to my information, I think it would be well worth while to investigate the matter and to keep the trade in the local territory as far as possible. I would ask of the minister that the matter be considered again and that it be given every possible favourable consideration.
Certainly, Mr. Chairman. If they are in a position to compete in the future, they will certainly get a chance for the business.
Will that opportunity be offered in the near future?
Oh, yes. These matters are continually under review. I know that tenders are called quite often.

Mr. Chairman, there are three different matters which I should like to place before the Minister of Defence Production, and I would appreciate having his comments on them. Yesterday, when the minister was
Supply-Defence Production introducing his estimates, as reported at page 4876 he said:
The situation the government faces in the immediate future is, however, one of preparing for either of two eventualities-all-out war or an extended period of peace.
I greatly doubt whether the minister's remark there was all-inclusive because I think the real situation we face is a prolonged period of being prepared to defend ourselves rather than a period of peace, if the minister meant it as an actual peace.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I meant war or no war.

Yes. I think that we should face the fact that we will either be in an all-out war-which all of us pray fervently can be avoided-or we will have to be in a state of preparation; and that is something entirely new for Canada as it is for the other freedom-loving nations.
I have been greatly impressed by a report tabled in the United States and known as the Vance report, with which no doubt the minister is familiar. As a matter of fact, the only copy I could get was obtained by the parliamentary library from the Department of Trade and Commerce. The report is entitled "Production Capacity: A Military Reserve. A Report to the Director of Defence Mobilization by the Advisory Committee on Production Equipment." In that report Mr. Vance and his associates point out clearly this new condition we are facing in these words, and I think the words apply to Canada as well as to the United States:
But now that forces in-being and production of weapons have been brought up to substantial levels, the emphasis should be shifted to completing the production capacity needed as a base for full mobilization.
The basic assumption we have accepted is that the nation must maintain a high level of military preparedness over a period of years-a wholly new concept in our history. To make acceptable and supportable a mobilization program based on this assumption, military preparedness must be attained with maximum economy and with a minimum drain on the nation's resources.
As the minister knows, the report goes on to point out the weaknesses in stockpiling; that is, in acquiring large stocks particularly of war materials. Mr. Vance points out that even the United States is not in a position to supply all the materials that would be needed for stockpiling, if that system is to be used rather than one of building up production capacity. He also points out that the system of stockpiling would entail great losses from obsolescence and-that the costs are much higher than they are in merely having production capacity. For example, he explains the difference with regard to tanks. He says:
When an Inventory of 5,000 tanks becomes totally obsolete, it means a loss of at least $1 billion, but
4922	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production
the cost of keeping the tank plant facilities up to date would be a small fraction of that amount.
I would hope that the minister would adopt a policy similar to that advocated in this report. Mr. Vance summed up his views in one paragraph where he said that the best interests of the nation would be served by substituting, to the greatest extent practicable, additional production facilities for stockpiles of military end items.
The minister in his statement yesterday said

he did not indicate that this was the plan being followed by Canada in full-that we were, as I understood him, and I may have been -wrong in interpreting his remarks, to go on manufacturing these articles and to hand them over to our associates in the North Atlantic treaty under a mutual aid program. I doubt very much whether the Canadian people should be faced with the cost of a plan of that kind, especially as it seems to be a good deal more expensive than merely having the productive capacity ready.
As I understand the Vance report, it is recommended that the government see to it that machine tools are acquired and that the plants themselves are ready or in such condition that they -can be set up quickly, rather than setting up plants and continuing to manufacture materials. The Canadian plan seems to involve the manufacture of materials and then giving these materials to others. That of course will put a strain on Canada's raw materials, and it will mean that the Canadian taxpayer will have to pay for all these materials which are turned over.
I ask the minister to clarify the situation in his department on that point. In connection therewith, and really ancillary to this point is-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Perhaps I might deal with that point for the moment.
All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My statement was:
The maintenance of these specialized facilities, which have been set up to meet potential requirements of the armed forces, presents difficult problems. Canada is not, of course, alone in facing these difficulties. In the United States, too, the authorities are greatly concerned. As a partial solution we are studying the possibility of maintaining certain of our production lines operating at minimum economic rates by offering the end items to our NATO allies-
The situation varies with different production lines. For example, automotive vehicles; the difficulty of shutting down a line of automotive vehicles and starting it up again when required is not great because the skills


remain in the plant. But we have one source of explosives, the government arsenal. It would be impossible to shut that plant down, disperse the skills and expect to start it up again when the war came. In the first place, the physical equipment would not be usable without extensive rehabilitation, and the skills would have to be collected from wherever they might have gone were the plant shut down. An explosive plant is a good example of the type of plant where it is better to keep its lines operating at minimum capacity, even if we have to give away the product, rather than close the plant down and disperse the skills. The raw materials that go into explosives are not expensive. The cost of making explosives is largely in the cost of the plant and the workmen to operate the plant; represented by labour and overhead. These are the chief costs, and they are costly.
There are various items-I do not know that I can give other examples of plants that could be kept going just about as cheaply as shutting them down with any idea that they must be rehabilitated and put back into operation on short notice. For instance, pic-rite; we are the sole producers of picrite in the British empire, in fact on the North American continent. We kept the picrite line going at minimum capacity for two or three years after the war and stored the material. Then there came a terrific demand for picrite, and now both Britain and the United States are pressing us to enlarge the picrite facility. Had we shut that facility down completely we would have been out of the picrite business, and someone else would have had to start from scratch. That I think explains the general problem if not in all its details.
You must take one particular type of production, then we can discuss whether it is cheaper in the long run to shut the plant down and disperse the skills or to keep the plant operating at minimum capacity.

I notice in the Vance report there is no example of end items on which production should be kept under way and the end items supplied to the other NATO nations. That seems to be a Canadian policy exclusively and different from the recommendations of the Vance report. I realize you cannot lay down any general policy that would cover every type of manufacture, but does the minister not think that basically our policy in this new type of period we are passing through should be one merely of preparing our productive capacity rather than of actually manufacturing the goods and

either stockpiling them here or sending them over to the other NATO nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not think you can answer that question categorically. In my opinion one of the strongest links in the defence of Canada is the capacity to produce on short notice. There is a limit, of course, to stockpiling. For instance, during the second world war, I think about 1943, we had an interruption to ocean transportation, and we filled the railroad right of way on both sides of the tracks from Windsor to Montreal with automotive vehicles and ammunition. That experience gives an idea of the problem of continuing stockpiling of production for any considerable time. As a matter of fact the stockpiling of end items beyond the immediate need for mobilization is of doubtful value anyway. Ammunition gets old and has to be destroyed, and other items lose their usefulness through obsolescence.
There is some misconception about stockpiling. The Department of Defence Production stockpiles raw materials such as tin or natural rubber or manganese, items that are not available if things in the Far East go wrong, but we do not store any manufactured item, at least no more than required to level out production. We do buy cloth in quantity, store it and distribute it for uniforms. We find that we can buy cloth much more cheaply if we can give our mills a good run on the type of cloth that is required for uniforms. But the mobilization stores carried by the services represent the equipment that is needed to permit immediate mobilization, and to provide for mobilization during the first six months. The time varies according to the item.
Have we not reached that stage already?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I rather think we have. That is not my business to know. I cannot say categorically that we have reached that stage, but I will assume that is the case. We all remember the early days of world war II- at least I have reason to do so-1939 and 1940, when we had troops going around without uniforms and with old shoes, or at least civilian shoes, and using something other than rifles to drill with. Well, no one wants that to happen again. And if immediate mobilization involves a division, we must have mobilization stocks to take care of that number of troops. The problem of stockpiling for that type of equipment is that of the army. The Department of Defence Production has a policy which involves the lowest stocks that can be carried to enable the department to function.
Supply-Defence Production
Why is there any need to buy large quantities of ordinary goods used by the civilian population?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is a problem for the Department of National Defence. I do not think it is possible for me to discuss it. I do not make that policy. Someone has asked why we need neckties. I have great confidence that men of experience are represented in the department of the quartermaster general in the army, and if they requisition neckties we do not question the need. It would upset the relations between the two departments if we questioned the requirements of the services, and it is not our business to do so. If the services say they need a gold-plated piano, it is our duty to buy it.
Surely not.

I have more confidence than that in the Minister of Defence Production. I would hate to be the person who sent in an order for a gold-plated piano. Is there any supervision exercised over this policy of piling up huge amounts of stores? For instance, I had a return showing the quantities of shaving brushes purchased since January 1 last year. I find that the minister's department since January 1, 1952, spent $128,849 on 138,748 brushes. Surely there is some authority which can decide whether the quartermaster general or the Department of National Defence is wasteful in ordering such huge quantities of these ordinary goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
In the first place, the requirements are screened in the Department of National Defence. Then every order is screened by treasury board; and there are special officers on treasury board whose duty it is to watch such requirements. If a question is raised the requisition is discussed with the Department of National Defence. My hon. friend will appreciate that our function as the procurement agency for the defence forces would not be consistent if we were to proceed to censor orders coming from the services. We have no specialists as to quantities needed by the services and we do not know what their requirements are. That is another line of business completely.
The rule is laid down in our department that if a requisition comes forward properly signed by the proper officers of the Department of National Defence, procurement is based upon that order. If treasury board believes the requisition is excessive, it will be stopped at treasury board level.

Then the responsibility for purchasing too large a quantity of these articles rests with treasury board. Is that correct?
4924	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It rests primarily with the Department of National Defence. As I say, treasury board has the ability to stop a purchase if it feels the expenditure is not made wisely.
I do not know whether the Minister of Defence Production is on treasury board or not,-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: In my 18 years as a member of the government I have never been on treasury board.

-but I do urge that he impress upon treasury board the need for cutting out such foolish purchases as 139,000 shaving brushes in a period of 15 months.
My next question has to do with steel. In the report of the department we find at page 16 a paragraph dealing with this subject. It explains that steel is in easier supply now than formerly. Then follows this paragraph:
However, in spite of this increase in Canadian production, the department anticipates that the demand for steel will continue to grow and that the level of imports from the United States, the United Kingdom and other countries will be maintained.
The minister's department is primarily responsible for the supply of steel obtained in Canada. Will he tell the committee what increase there will be during the present calendar year in Canadian steel producing capacity?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The production potential for 1955 is forecast at 4,800,000 tons of steel ingots.
That is for the year 1955?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes. Production today is hovering around 4,500,000 tons.
And what is it to be in 1955?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is to be 4,800,000 tons. At the present time consumption is about 5,500,000 tons. But there are certain types of steel Canada would never set out to produce. I have in mind, for instance, very heavy structural members. We have never supplied our full requirements, and I do not know that it is advisable to do so. It is just as well to have a margin of tonnage that we import in good times, and do not require to import in poor times-just a little cushion for our steel industry, which has a rather restricted market.
Do I understand there is to be an increase of only 300,000 tons in steel making capacity between 1953 and 1955?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is all we know at the present time.

Is there not some way in which that production can be increased? Surely, whether we are preparing for war or whether


all our international troubles are settled and we have reached an ordinary peacetime atmosphere, we would require far more than an increase of 300,000 tons in that period of years.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
My hon. friend will appreciate that we have just finished an increased production capacity of about 1,500,000 tons, which increased our former capacity by 50 per cent. That was a very large increase in one jump.
I understand why the steel mills would want to absorb -that new capacity before they move on to another general increase.

What is the situation now in connection with the establishment of a steel industry on the west coast? The provincial mines minister in British Columbia announced on May 2 that Frobisher Limited were going to establish a steel smelter on the west coast. Can the minister give any information on that?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I cannot; I have not heard anything about it.

Is there any possibility of Canada establishing plants to turn our iron ore from the Quebec-Labrador area into the meta-l form? When Dr. George S. Hume, director of scientific services for the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, made a speech on March 9, 1953, to the prospectors and developers association and the geological association of Canada, he said this:
It is suggested as not beyond the possibilities of our research scientists to find ways and means in Canada to utilize electric power and iron ore occurring together in the same area to at least effect a partial processing which would be of immense benefit to this country. The Ontario research foundation has been doing excellent work on the study of iron and our mines branch at Ottawa has a number of scientists well versed in the technology of treatment of all kinds of ores. Thus well directed efforts might accomplish much toward reducing our iron ore to the metal before shipment outside Canada just as we produce metal from our copper, nickel, lead and zinc ores for the most part in this country.
Has the government any such plan in mind at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The government of Canada has never been in the primary steel business and I would hope that it never will be. The production of steel is definitely a matter for private enterprise.
Apparently it involves research. Is research of this type being carried on?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Research of the type my hon. friend mentions is well advanced. It is now possible to smelt steel by electricity using a minimum of coke. That process has been considered in plans for the recent expansion in Canada but for this country at least, it has been found to be not as economical as the old

method. I believe it is in use in Norway. I do not think the metallurgical process is particularly difficult. As a matter of fact, at Trail they have been working on the metallurgical process of smelting their ores by electricity for some time.

My final question has to do with the matter of spreading contracts across the country. As the minister knows, for many years we have been complaining about the concentration of industries in the two central provinces. 1 have an example here of a situation which I think could be remedied by the minister. Within the last week or two tenders have been called for what are known as pallets and picture frames, the tender number being R.20-K-1727.
These pallets are for army use in Montreal, and London, Ontario. Apparently they are used to store goods on in the stockrooms. Goods are piled on these wooden pallets and they are thus more easily moved from place to place.
The specifications call for the use of hardwood, which means that firms, not only in British Columbia but on the prairies, cannot compete because they would have to buy their hardwood in Ontario, bring it across the country, process it and then send it back for army use at Montreal and London. The companies on the west coast contend that softwood could be used just as well as hardwood for these pallets and would be just as serviceable. I understand that both the air force and the navy use softwood pallets, but for some reason the army insists upon hardwood. The result is that these western firms are put in an impossible position to compete, and the amounts involved are quite substantial, being I beli'eve in the neighbourhood of $500,000.
This is one type of article that could be made on the west coast. Could the minister have the situation looked into and, I would hope, make a change so that softwood would be considered acceptable for these pallets for use by the army, just as it is for use by the other services?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The question of pallets came to my attention two years ago when we had an order to be delivered on the west coast. To my horror I found that they were being made in Toronto and the price delivered on the west coast was about one-half what it would be for the same article made in Vancouver. I inquired into it and the reason given was the same as that given by my hon. friend, that the army insisted upon hardwood pallets. Hardwood is not indigenous to the west coast.
Since then we have taken up the matter with the army every time an order for pallets was received, but they still insist that their pallets should be made of hardwood. They
Supply-Defence Production contend that softwood splinters too easily and will not stand up to service. As I explained to my hon. friend, we do not argue with the army about quantities. We sometimes argue about specifications, but the decision of the user is final. Unless the army can be persuaded to change its mind about pallets we must buy according to the specifications that are submitted to us.
I have a complaint against the navy as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member had better wait until the Minister of National Defence is here.

I received an answer from the Minister of Defence Production in reply to a question I had asked about Kindorf fittings for the navy. Orders were placed for these fittings in Montreal by what is called the lead yard. Apparently the Vickers people were the lead yard and they placed an order for these fittings which were to be placed in vessels on the west coast. The agents for Kindorf fittings in Vancouver were done out of this business because the order went through Montreal. The price to the government would have been exactly the same if ordered from the Vancouver agents. What procedure is followed in a case like that? Could there not be some system worked out whereby goods of that kind could be purchased from business people on the west coast?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am told that in this particular case the Kindorf people themselves did not wish to use their agents who handled civilian work. They have representatives in Montreal who handle naval work exclusively and they insisted that the business be put through those representatives. We did not care what agent handled the business as long as the price was the same, but the manufacturers insisted that we deal through the Montreal agent.
What is the policy of the department with regard to having goods of that type purchased where the ships are to be built?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We try to do that. Our policy is to buy as cheaply as possible. While there may be some hope of persuading the army to use softwood pallets, I do not think there is much hope of persuading the navy to use anything that is not according to naval tradition.

Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee on defence expenditure I want to make a few brief remarks before this item is passed. I want to say that the hon. member for Melfort, who was my colleague on this committee, and I attempted in
4926	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production every conceivable way to be as objective as possible in our approach to this question, which is the usual position of the party to which I belong. Our appeal to the electors has always been based on a basic political philosophy and program. We do not appeal to the electorate with a string of political negations that are often reshuffled to suit the necessities occasioned by a changing political climate and circumstance.
On that account we try to be as fair as we can. Before I proceed I do want to say that I think the chairman of the committee was quite fair. He gave us every opportunity to ask questions and there was a full discussion of each item. There was an unusually high attendance in the committee by members of all parties. Hon. members did the best they could to nibble away at the mountain of paper and information that was brought before them, but the committee had a mammoth and impossible task as far as completing its work was concerned. I do think we did the best we could in the time we had.
Last night I heard one of my Progressive Conservative friends to my right say that when the committee concluded its sittings he was frustrated. If the hon. gentleman would not mind taking a bit of advice from a backwoodsman and an unsophisticated backbencher, I would suggest that no one ever becomes frustrated if he is fully conversant with his own limitations and with the limitations of time and circumstance.
Before proceeding, Mr. Chairman, I must say that while we have had many sound criticisms from this side of the house, I cannot agree with some of the criticisms that have come from the Progressive Conservatives to my right. I think that in some cases they have been somewhat unfair and, as I look at the massive and immobile physique of the Minister of Defence Production, after listening to some of these minor and trifling criticisms, I am reminded of a story I read about a small boy throwing peanuts at the rock of Gibraltar in an effort to demolish it.
Mr. Chairman, I think the committee had an impossible task but it did the best it could. Look at the agenda which the committee had before it:	1. Acquisition and leases-land
and buildings at Esquimalt, Rocky Point and Gagetown, by the Department of National Defence; 2. A general statement with particular reference to Penhold, Namao, Churchill, Cold Lake, Esquimalt, Rocky Point and Gagetown, by the president of Defence Construction Limited; 3. Married quarters program, by president, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.


The following topics were also suggested:
1. Armaments, tanks, ammunition, guns and small arms; 2. Naval vessels; 3. Operation Pine Tree; 4. Training costs-all services; 5. Recruiting costs; 6. Soft goods; 7. Military travelling costs.
Well, Mr. Chairman, of all those we were only able to deal with the Currie report and the question of defence construction. As far as the departmental officials are concerned, we in this group recognize that they were willing to answer all questions. There were a lot of questions answered and a great deal of material was provided. In answering written questions and verbal questions by members of the committee, in my opinion the officials demonstrated that they had a very complete grasp of the department they were administering.
As I said in a previous debate, these increased costs-and we do think there were increased costs, that there was waste and that there was some inefficiency, and I think members of the committee should be frank and admit it, because there is no use trying to say there was not-were caused by factors beyond the control of these very capable and hard-working officials. They had no control over shortages which caused delays and obviously increased costs. No one can deny that. There were many changes in plans on the part of the army which increased costs, and weather conditions caused losses. Attempts to work overtime and attempts to overcome the weather and that sort of thing caused some extra expense. There was a shortage of satisfactory supervisory staff. Everyone in this country knows how difficult it is to get experienced and competent architects and experienced and competent engineers, and qualified staff of that type. Labour difficulties often arose. Above all there were repeated changes of plans by the Department of National Defence and an overriding sense of urgency which permeated the whole building program. I think we must fairly recognize those factors. The officials had little or no control over them and we must recognize that those factors were the cause of certain increased costs, certain inefficiency and certain waste.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, the members of this group cannot support the report presented by the majority of the committee because we recognize those facts and we think they are not fully or sufficiently recognized in the report by the majority. No more can we support the report-shall I say the unofficial minority report-presented by the Progressive Conservatives, because theirs was a political approach to the question from the

opposite side. As I say, we have tried to look at this question fairly and objectively.
My further remarks are going to be brief, but I do want to make this point. We can do very little at this time to correct errors, inefficiency and waste of the past, but these expenditures are going to continue. I think that something will have been accomplished as a result of the discussions in this house and during the sittings of the committee if the government takes further steps to protect the taxpayers' interests in these expenditures. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, my colleague the member for Melfort last night put on the record a constructive suggestion which he moved as a resolution in the committee. We tried to get majority support for that resolution in the committee but we were unsuccessful. I will read the resolution which my colleague moved in the committee and then make some comments about it. He moved:
Your committee recommends that parliament should ask the Auditor General to establish three teams of auditors, one for each branch of the services, navy, army and air force, to make such check audits of military establishments as are necessary to determine that proper stocktaking is being carried out and that proper records are being kept, also to determine the physical conditions of all stores and whether proper storage and maintenance methods are being followed, and that the Auditor General report the findings of these teams to parliament at regular intervals of not less than six months.
My colleague repeated that plea in his remarks last evening, but I thought there was not a very favourable response from the Minister of Defence Production. I think that was because he possibly did not quite understand what we were proposing in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend misunderstood my reference. Someone said there should be an independent check by parliament and I pointed out that it is the duty of the Auditor General, who is an officer of parliament, to make that check. I think I made no derogatory reference to the proposal that the Auditor General set up teams to do so. That would not have been my business.
I would like to see the Auditor General make the most accurate check that can be made of the army stores, and if your method is the one he considers best, then I am all for it.

We are delighted to notice the open mind which the minister has in this connection.
We believe that one of the very necessary things and one of the most important things is that these stockpiles of goods come more
Supply-Defence Production directly under the control of parliament. In that connection and in support of our proposal I wish to quote briefly from the Auditor General's report for 1952, page 24, paragraphs 57 and 58. He there is dealing with this very situation on which we based our resolution or recommendation. I read:
57.	In order that any sudden international emergency will not find the country unprepared, Canada, for the first time in peacetime, has large permanent service forces and a declared public policy to accumulate holdings of supplies of all kinds, to establish permanent depots, etc. Consequently, a large investment is represented by stores for (a) current needs, and (b) an emergency.
58.	Once procurement has been completed, it is the practice in some commonwealth countries to regard issues for immediate requirements of the services as outside parliament's concern; all other holdings are regarded as still of parliamentary interest. The reasoning is aptly stated in Colonel Durell's book, "Parliamentary Grants," which he wrote when chief paymaster of the war office. He states: "Parliament in granting the money to purchase stores does so on the understanding that the stores shall be used for the purposes for which they are intended when the grant is asked for. Any other application of them is as much a misappropriation as if the grant itself were applied to another purpose than the purchase of stores.
Should this view be regarded as suited to Canadian requirements, attention is drawn to the need for the establishing of a dividing line between service and departmental accounting responsibilities.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we in this group believe that is a very sound recommendation. Once again we urge the government to consider it. We are concerned about these large stockpiles, over which we believe parliament should have more effective and more direct control.
That is about all I am going to say at this time. We urge the consideration of our proposal by the house and the minister. It is intended as a step towards the development of a system of supervision that will make as certain as humanly possible that the taxpayer gets full value for his money in the large spending of this department.

I wish to thank the hon. member for Kootenay West for his kind references and his objective analysis. If in the course of my few remarks I make some caustic comments, they are not applicable to him or his party.
The committee on defence expenditure was first appointed on January 22, and it held 26 meetings. It is fair for me to say to the house that, under the present circumstances, human ingenuity could not have devised a unanimous report. What troubles me particularly is the reference made by my impetuous friend, the hon. member for Eglin-ton, to the fact that the committee's report was a whitewash. This comment was later
4928	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production echoed by the leader of the Social Credit party. There can be no denial that I am a party man, but I have never been a party hack. In my 25 years of political life I have had some small reputation for independence. I am not easily taken in. I would not be party to a whitewash. I am not now, and that is the reason I rise to make these few remarks.
The committee was set up for the purpose of seeking out, and if necessary ferreting out the facts without endangering national security. In the committee information was easily obtainable. All one had to do was ask for it. We have a thousand pages of evidence in the committee reports. The information was produced quickly and accurately. If I recall correctly, the hon. member for Calgary East last year said that we gave too much information. He got lost in it. I think some of us got lost in it, too. Last night the hon. member for York West said we had given too much information. As a matter of fact he stated that there was an avalanche of paper and a Niagara of information; colourful, but true. The hon. member who just sat down said there was a mountain of paper information. My point is that if a member of the committee asked a question, he got an answer.
On the other hand we have the very able hon. member for Greenwood who, in speaking last night, had a different slant on it. He said that the defence expenditure committee turned down everything asked for. Surely you cannot have it both ways. Either you got information or you did not get information. We must be clear about it. Nothing was concealed and nothing was denied which it was within the competence of this committee to deliver.
Perhaps it would be interesting for this house to learn that no defence committee in Great Britain or the United States received as much information publicly as did this committee on defence expenditure. It has never been the practice at Westminster or in this House of Commons to produce the records of courts of inquiry. They have been denied on the floor of this house time and again, yet we produced them for the defence expenditure committee. It has never been the practice at Westminster or in this house to produce the records of courts martial, but we produced them in the defence expenditure committee. It has never been the practice at Westminster or in this house to produce auditors' reports, but we produced excerpts from auditors' reports for the defence expenditure committee.
You may ask, why, and under what authority, was this done? I am not so sure of the authority, but we felt it was in the
[Mr. Croll.l

public interest that the information be produced and it was produced. It was a precedent, a historic precedent, and I think it is worth while for this house to know about it.
At the sessions of the committee last year we covered a great deal of the subject matter that was covered in yesterday's discussions. Yesterday the hon. member for Eglinton placed on the record a list of goods, quantities and costs, as appears on page 4878 of Hansard for May 6, 1953. Well, the scale of issue and the scale of distribution is not new. We did not go into it again this year because our program in the committee this year was dictated not by the great Liberal majority on the committee, but by the opposition. At the first meeting of the agenda committee we asked the members what matters they wanted particularly, and it was at the suggestion of the opposition that construction was to head the list. Then there would be armament, tanks, ammunition, guns, small arms, naval vessels and then "Operation Pine Tree". I asked them what "Operation Pine Tree" was, because I am frank to admit I did not know. The next items were to be training costs and recruiting costs.
Finally the very influential chairman was able to get an item on the list of matters to be considered, and I thought we should discuss soft goods. The hon. member for Skeena was then able to get military travel costs on the agenda. We spelled it out even a little better than that. You can recognize, from what we decided to investigate, who particularly asked that these matters be investigated. The first thing we were to do was deal with Esquimalt, Rocky Point and Gagetown. Then we were to deal with Penhold, Namao, Churchill, Cold Lake, Esquimalt, Rocky Point and Gagetown in more precise fashion.
Quite a number of speeches have been made in the House of Commons by the hon. member for Red Deer and the hon. member for Greenwood with respect to construction. If there is one criticism I have of the committee, and I do not criticize the members as such because I have not had the experience of sitting in opposition, it is that I find-
You will have.

Not for a long time, my friend. I find that the last thing my friends want is the facts. They attend for the purpose of affirming the things they are talking about, and if they do not get that information they immediately shift ground and want to devote their attention to something else entirely. There can be no denial that we investigated the spending of a great deal of money. We spent that money on the boys and girls in our

services. We spent it in order to attract them to the services and in order that they might have conditions comparable to those which they would have in civilian life. That is the least they are entitled to get, and they will get that from this government. We intend to continue to feed them, to clothe them and provide security for them. If there is anyone in this country who has any other way of dealing with the problem, we should like to hear about it.
Hon. members have expressed some disappointment over the method of parliamentary inquiry. I know only two methods of parliamentary inquiry. For the moment I will not discuss what happens to the opposition behind the iron curtain; I do not think it is applicable. But we have the parliamentary system that the Americans use, and the British and Canadian parliamentary system of inquiry. I am told that if you conduct a proper inquiry in the United States, the chairman must wear a coon cap and must be televised. Then you must have these breathless announcements by radio commentators, with appropriate commercials about lazy laxatives. Statements are made by committee members and sometimes they even permit a witness to speak, although I am not sure about that.
I appreciate the fact that the chairman of this committee disappointed some hon. members in that he did not make headlines, and up to this moment he does not know whether he is "telegenic". However, there was one thing we did. We had a normal inquiry under British and Canadian parliamentary practices. The evidence was given; the evidence was assessed, and it is now before this committee. When I hear the word "whitewash" it surprises me no little. If on the part of the majority there had been any desire to whitewash, we would have presented to that committee a report as phony as the one that was presented by the Conservative group.
Oh, oh.
Go easy.

The report that was presented was factual, with one conclusion which was fully warranted. In the report we did not spare the government. In our report we said that Mr. Currie-and we dealt with the Currie aspects of it first-had made certain recommendations in parts 2, 3 and 4 and that those recommendations had been accepted by the government. There was endorsation of the recommendations for improving the Department of National Defence. We said there had been some irregularities in the accounting methods but that no dishonesty was involved, and that the omission resulted largely from
Supply-Defence Production the urgency of requirements, following the outbreak of hostilities in Korea.
There was no denial that methods might well be improved. But one of the things that we were particularly anxious to incorporate into the report was the fact that Mr. Currie did not see Petawawa alone but saw nine of the largest camps in Canada, and that only at Petawawa did he find what he set out in what became part of his report, but which was not as the result of research by himself or his staff but as the result of information which came to him and which later proved to be untrue. You could find proof of that in the evidence half a dozen times.
In so far as the construction aspect of it was concerned, it is interesting to see how much work we actually did. We had before us 894 construction contracts involving $375-8 million. They involved 172 sites and 1,270 buildings. On top of that we had 533 contracts with consulting engineers, architects, surveyors and what-not involving $13-7 million. That made almost $400 million in all. That is the amount of work that was before the committee at the present sittings.
I think one of the things that should be brought to the attention of the committee is the method of operation of the Department of Defence Production. Here is what they had to say. In the matter of publicly advertised tenders, they were opened in the presence of a committee composed of the regional engineer, regional superintendent and regional secretary of the regional office of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in the region concerned, and after the awarding of the contracts each tenderer was advised by letter of the order of his bidding. That is a practice that is not usually followed, but certainly anyone who does business under those circumstances is not attempting to hide anything.
We heard the hon. member for Wetaskiwin deal yesterday with the matter of excessive costs. If you take the trouble to read the amendment of the Conservative members of the committee-and it will be trouble- you will find that in that report there is also a reference to the same item of $28,254.67. We dealt with $400 million in contracts, and we kept saying to them, "Where is this waste, this extravagance and this inefficiency?" Finally they both hit upon the same idea. Both came to the same conclusion. The Tories first mentioned the fact that there was a $28,000 item. Then my friend from the Social Credit party did the same thing.
In the light of the amount of money that was spent, surely there is ample justification for saying that the Canadian people received

Supply-Defence Production value for their money it all they can point to is the item of $28,254, which is made up in this fashion. In the fall of 1951 the R.C.A.F. requested a speed-up operation at Penhold involving extra work shifts, in order to complete certain buildings by February, 1952. This operation was cancelled on December 11 when it became obvious that the desired results could not be achieved. Extra cost involved was $28,254.67. Evidence was brought out that good judgment was used in incurring this expenditure and also in cancelling the arrangement when it become apparent that the full hopes for the benefit could not be obtained. What happened was that when it was found they were not obtaining the results they thought they might, they cancelled the arrangement.
This talk about a Liberal majority, and imposing upon the house and the committee and giving the impression that this is a most unusual method of conducting business, is not unusual. Every committee in every parliament reflects the house. May I tell my hon. friends that in Ontario they will find that the committee will have a majority of Conservatives; and in Saskatchewan, as my friends already know, the premier of that province keeps a majority of C.C.F. members on committees there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The people keep them there.
Tucker does not enjoy having them there. The people keep us here, as my hon. friend well knows. The same thing applies. The same situation is reflected in Great Britain and in the United States.
There is some sense of independence there on the part of members.
There was a sense of independence on our part, as my hon. friend well knows.
No, I do not know that.

My hon. friend knows full well that the final report was attractive to some of the members of the committee; they were not Conservative members, but the report was certainly attractive and it was factual. There was only one conclusion that could be put in the report, and the conclusion was justified. What my hon. friends wanted us to do was walk into the defence department and use a meat axe on them, and in that way we would have crippled the department and crippled the armament program of this country.
Can we get back to facts?

We have been on facts, my friend. It is hard for you to recognize them; that is the only thing. Let me just say that


when we deal with facts this Liberal government makes no claim to perfection in its record. Infallibility and perfection belong to the Tories and with that 18 years of opposition and more to come. We do not claim that we have spent millions of dollars of public funds without loss due to human frailty. We have made some errors in judgment. There have been errors in the expenditure of public money. There has been some criminality, and the people responsible have been punished.
Who?

Well, they are in jail. I do not know their names. There has been nothing to support the charge of waste, extravagance and inefficiency. It is now becoming not only a slogan without meaning, but it is becoming self-destructive.
It is beginning to hurt you.
Not a bit.
Oh, is it not?

Listen to what I have to say. We had a committee on defence expenditure in 1951; we had a committee again in 1952 and we had a committee in 1953. In these three years the committee dealt with nearly all of five or six billion dollars, or the best part of it. In all that time, with a full, complete and open hearing and with people on the other side looking for trouble, none was found. The Leader of the Opposition spent some time on that committee in the early stages, but he could find nothing there at all. Unlike the situation in the United States, there are no minks and no pinks; there are no deep freezes; there are no five percenters; no influence peddlers; no double dealing. There were honest mistakes and we admitted them, and they will not be repeated. It is regrettable that the Department of National Defence is turned into a playing field for purely political campaigns, with the Currie report as the football.
I am not speaking about honest criticism. Goodness knows, the Department of National Defence can take it, and some of the other departments can take it. I am talking about these irresponsible attacks, wilfully misleading statements, whose sole purpose is to convert our defence program into a playground for party politics. We have heard a great deal of the Currie report; we shall hear more about it in the months ahead. I wonder if it would not be interesting for the committee to have the second section of the Currie report which some hon. members have not seen. I am reading from the Toronto Star of May 4.
Oh, oh.
It appeared in all the papers.
This must be the second Currie report; the first one disappeared.

This is the item:
George S. Currie, author of the Currie report on the army works service of the Department of National Defence, paid an outstanding tribute to Hon. Brooke Claxton, Minister of National Defence, here Saturday.
I quote:
I would also like at this time to thank the member of parliament in whose constituency we are now standing and who represents us at Ottawa with such competence, such industry and such integrity.
Hon. Brooke Claxton has grown up amongst us and thus we are all most conscious of the magnificent way in which he has represented us, not only as regards our own affairs, but as a Canadian giving outstanding service to our country.
What concerns the Canadian people-and you will find it out when you get to the hustings-
You will find it out, too.
We are very anxious to go. You are the ones who are complaining.
And worrying about the date.
What concerns the Canadian people is that this government is not dodging responsibilities, and is not looking for scapegoats. Every one of us here is prepared to take his responsibility.
Oh, oh.

I did not hear what was said, so I cannot reply. Whatever situation was found that needed correction was not only localized but corrected and cleaned up. They have the undertaking of this government that it will not occur again.
Glossed it all over.
Put the lid on.
That is all.
Closed the door.
We closed the door to horses and to people like yourself.
Did you see the cartoon of yourself in the Globe and Mail?

I enjoyed it. I thought they did pretty well. It was not too handsome, but that is not their fault; they are doing the best they can. I am not going to say very much more except to indicate that yesterday an hon. member of the Social Credit party raised the question of the Alexander Construction company. He did not raise it in the committee. He asked a few questions, and when the answer was not what he expected, when the name of the Alexander
Supply-Defence Production Construction company did not come to the fore, he lost all interest.
What surprised me was that the hon. mefn-ber for York West yesterday rose in the house and in a very loud voice chastised us for not dealing with aircraft production. He sat through 19 meetings-I had to count them today in order to make sure-and never once did he say a word about aircraft production during the course of those meetings.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the question of the production of aircraft never came before the committee. It was on the agenda, but we were dealing with construction items such as the building of barracks blocks and all that sort of thing, and we never got to it. We never did deal with the whole problem of aircraft production. And it was in my opinion deliberately done; it was a deliberate avoidance by the committee, in that we did not deal with the whole question of arms production.
And also on a question of privilege-
Order.
Mr. Speaker, I have the floor.
On a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Eglinton I understand is raising a point of order.
Yes, on a matter of privilege.
There is a difference.
The record shows-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is not privilege; you are out of order.
There seems to be a great deal of prophecy on the other side of the house. I had only two words out of my mouth and the Minister of National Health and Welfare is prepared to rule.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have known you for a quarter of a century.
With respect to this matter of aircraft production, the fact is that when we closed off on construction, the record shows-and I think the hon. member will admit it-that I pled-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Pleaded.
-with the chairman and the committee to have, even at the expense of a night sitting, an opportunity to deal with aircraft production. We pleaded with him to have meetings to consider it.

What the hon. member says is correct. The hon. member for Eglinton did not plead, but he did ask, he did suggest that

Supply-Defence Production we hold a few meetings on aircraft production. Quite right. I am not talking about the hon. member for Eglinton; I shall deal with him later.
I am talking about the hon. member for York West. I am speaking for myself and for the committee. He spoke last night-you heard him-
And spoke very well.

Referring to the hon. member for York West, we had a meeting on January 27; he was a member of the committee, but he was not present. At that time we did bring in a report, and the second item of the report was aircraft production. Whether he knew about it or not, he certainly must have read the minutes. But he never once raised that point until he rose in the House of Commons and brought it out, when he thought he would not be corrected.
In so far as the hon. member for Eglinton is concerned, he did suggest that we deal with the matter of aircraft production. I pointed out to him that we had not completed the construction program. I do not think we had touched or that we had finished with Esquimau. It seemed that if we continued on construction it would be endless. There was item after item we ought to have dealt with, but there seemed to be no purpose in opening up something new when we could not follow it up. I suggested that it be brought up on the minister's estimates; that the minister's estimates had not yet been passed, and he could obtain the information here.
The hon. member is quite right, and I have no quarrel with him at all about it. My quarrel is this, that on the one hand we have the hon. member for York West, the hon. member for Calgary East, the hon. member for Kootenay West and other hon. members who say, "We could not get anything done on the committee. We were just flooded with information." They do not suggest it was by design. Then on the other hand the hon. member for Greenwood in his own bailiwick says, "We could not get information out of that committee." We have, on still the other hand, the hon. member for Eglinton who says, "I wanted aircraft production discussed", and I do not deny that. But the hon. member for York West, on the other hand, never once mentioned it. You cannot have it both ways all the time.

On a point of order, the agenda committee set out what items we were going to deal with, and they set them out in chronological order. Aircraft production was not reached. Had it been reached we could
(Mr. Croll.]
have dealt more usefully with the questions of the main expenditures on defence.
I was not on the agenda committee, but this is what happened. We pleaded with the committee to hold night sittings and to hold extra sittings so we could get on with the job and get through the work of the committee. But that was denied us. And if there is any reason that we did not get to aircraft production and the production of arms, the government members of the committee must accept the entire and complete blame for it.

The hon. member for Eglinton spoke to me about holding sittings, but I never heard the expression "night sittings". The one reason we did not hold further sittings at that time was that the broadcasting committee was sitting, the Criminal Code committee was sitting and the committee on industrial relations was sitting, and members were jumping from committee to committee. You just could not divide yourself up into enough pieces to sit on all the committees. I never heard the suggestion about a night committee, because the house was sitting all the time.

Let me say this, because the hon. member for Spadina has referred to the agenda committee. I was one of the two Progressive Conservative members on that committee on the agenda, and it was I who asked that agenda committee, at an early date, that aircraft production be one item we should consider. I did so, I may say, at the request of the hon. member for York West. There was a list of nine subjects altogether and, in the time at our disposal, although we met twice a week regularly, we covered just the first two of those nine. Aircraft production was third, and we fell short of it.
It appears that the Flemings talk only to the Crolls, and the Adamsons don't talk to either of them. There is nothing we can do about it.
Had we brought it up we would have been ruled out of order anyway by the hon. member who is speaking to the committee at this time.

The hon. member for York West does a fairly good job of speaking for himself, but he has never been very successful in speaking for the hon. member for Spadina. Let me assure the hon. member that the only time he was ruled out of order was when he wanted to be ruled out of order, and he did it deliberately. That is why he was ruled out of order. I have said all I wish to say, and-

On a point of order. I was never ruled out of order in the committee.

The party was ruled out of order, and every motion we made to go into these things was ruled out of order.
Well, if you were not ruled out of order, what are you complaining about?
Merely to keep the record straight.
Let us see if the record speaks for itself or not. If the hon. member has taken the time to read the report made by the committee of which he was a member-
The majority report.

-he will have seen what I shall now read. He can read it, if he wants to.
In one case your committee voted not to call for reports ruled outside its terms of reference by the chairman and in another case voted not to call for certain reports of the chief auditor of the Department of National Defence. Summaries of these auditor's reports were tabled and the chief auditor gave evidence that they constituted a fair summary.
That was the only time anyone was ever ruled out of order in that committee, and it was stated in the report because it was a factual matter.
It was by the majority of the committee.
Come to the point.

I have said all I wish to say, or at least almost all I wish to say. Let me say in closing that I believe, all in all, the committee worked as hard as it possibly could and did as much work as it could have been expected to do. We did have a great deal of information. The difficulty with the committee is that we did not really appreciate what $400 million means. When we got into it we found that there was far more work than we anticipated. With all the good will in the world there is just so much you can do. Members did ask questions and as a result they got answers. As a result of that there were more questions and more answers. It was a big task. I read the record and I am sure no one else did, but as chairman I had to do it. It took hours and hours after the committee was over just to go through the record of the evidence and glance at the various appendices and exhibits. That entailed a great deal of work. I think the committee did good work in 1951; it did good work in 1952, and it did good work in 1953.
The committee hearings have been disappointing to some opposition members. What they were looking for was not there. It never was. Nobody hid it. Nobody took it away.
I can assure hon. members of the committee that we who sit on the government side have no idea what evidence will be presented
Supply-Defence Production from day to day. The first time we hear these matters is when they are presented to the committee. We deal with the evidence in the same fashion that other hon. members have to. Some of it is surprising; some of it is puzzling; some of it we question. I believe the members of the committee, no matter to what party they belonged, were trying to be as helpful as they possibly could and endeavoured in every way they could to indicate in some fashion how to reduce the costs of the defence department without impairing its efforts.
I think this committee has had a good effect. I think the committee sitting has had a salutary effect upon the Department of National Defence. We shall reap the benefits of it in days to come. I would ask my hon. friends in the days ahead when they are talking about the Department of National Defence to talk from information rather than imagination.
Would the hon. member tell me if the number of Liberals on the committee was out of proportion to the number here in the house?
I understand it was the same proportion that is normal on every committee.

Mr. Chairman, a few
minutes ago there was quite a lot of talk about keeping the record straight, but I fear that after the speech just made by the hon. member for Spadina the record will be so tangled up that it will never be straightened out again. However, I shall do my best to untangle a few knots.
I do not intend at this date in the session to take up time by going into the details of the evidence given before the defence expenditure committee this year, nor do I intend to go over the report submitted to the house by that committee clause by clause in order to show why I consider that in many respects it is a whitewash. I do not think it is necessary to go over it in detail in that way, because the members of the official opposition who were members of the committee moved an amendment to the report which is now public property and which sets forth our views as to what kind of report should have been presented.
The hon. member for Spadina seemed to take considerable objection to the fact that the hon. member for Eglinton and one or two others said this report constituted a whitewash. I do not know why he should have taken such objection. As I said, I am not going to go over the report clause by clause, but as it was read I marked certain sentences and statements to which I think

Supply-Defence Production that word would apply and to which at least I took violent exception. There were some ten of them that I marked as illustrations of what I mean. The first sentence to which I should like to refer appears on page 2 of the report and reads:
All information requested by your committee was made available by the Department of National Defence, defence production and appropriate crown companies.
The information asked for by the committee was not made available. We asked for auditor's reports. We did not get them; all we got were excerpts. The hon. member for Kamloops-
If the hon. member will permit me, just to keep the record straight, certain members of the committee asked for it, but the committee itself did not ask for that information from the department.
That is exactly the whole tone of this report. That is mere verbal quibbling.
Not at all.

That is exactly the sort of thing I object to. There are statements in this report which from the strictly legalistic point of view might be said to indicate what happened, but they give an absolutely false impression.

On a point of order, it is not fair to impute that the Department of National Defence, the Department of Defence Production or crown companies refused any information, because that is literally and actually not true. Information that was requested officially by the committee was given.

I did not say that the defence department or defence production or crown companies had refused information. What happened was that the chairman and the Liberal majority on the committee refused to have information produced because they thought it might do them some harm.
Over and over again.

This sentence I think gives a false impression and I object to it. I object to it particularly because of the grounds on which the parliamentary assistant has just defended it. The second sentence on the next page reads as follows:
The total losses due to the thefts at Camp Petawawa after recoveries amounted to less than $36,000.
Again a completely false impression. In his report Mr. Currie said it was impossible to determine the amount of the losses, and as an example he indicated how he had tried over a considerable period to find the facts


in connection with the bags of cement. He said that although he had had a number of men trying to track down the 18,000 odd bags of cement which it was estimated were missing or were concerned, it was impossible to determine that even after a most painstaking investigation. He gave other instances. He said it was impossible to determine the monetary loss. He went on further to say that apart from the monetary loss, the losses as a result of bad administration and so on were considerably greater than any direct monetary loss which might have been suffered.
The effect of putting a statement of this sort in the report is to try to persuade this house and the people of Canada that the only loss suffered at Petawawa was the small amount of $36,000. That is not what Mr. Currie said. That is not the fact. It is a complete misrepresentation of the Currie report and of the facts in the case.
As I say, I do not want to take up the time of the committee by going into the other eight instances, but they are all along the same lines. It is in view of that fact that I say the report was a whitewash as far as these ten instances are concerned. I think perhaps more than that might be found.
As I say, the hon. member for Spadina took considerable objection to the statement that it was a whitewash, and he made a great point of the fact that the report that we concurred in was a political document while the report put in by himself was not a political document. I think the speech he made would convince anyone who listened to it or who reads it that the hon. member for Spadina does not frequently speak in a non-political way. If that was a non-political speech then I do not know what a political speech would sound like. I am not condemning the hon. member for making a political speech.
It was a good one.

I do not blame him for doing it, but I do blame him for trying to pretend that his report was a non-political report. It was just about as political as he could get it. He said that if they had wanted to turn in a political report it would have been very different. I would ask the question: How political can you get? It might have been a little different, but it could not have been very much different. I think he just about plumbed the depths as far as political reports are concerned in the one he turned in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The laughter sounds very hollow.
You cannot even laugh now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Be careful.

I do not know why the hon. member for Spadina should have wrought himself up into such an appearance of indignation over the fact that politics have entered into this matter, particularly in view of his own speech and his own report. I leave the matter at that point.
The hon. member for Spadina said great quantities of information were supplied to the committee. That is correct; I agree with that. Vast quantities of information were supplied to the committee. As a matter of fact the same thing was true last year and I said so then. The point I complained about last year and about which I complain again, in so far as information supplied to the committee is concerned, is that a great deal of the information supplied covered minor details and was in fact a waste of time to the committee. As a matter of fact, I think that a great amount of paper was deliberately shot at us last year and this year so it would not be possible for us to carry on the investigation which we should have been able to carry on.
You asked for it.

In other words, there was a deliberate policy of smothering us with innumerable small details. The hon. member for Spadina in his speech quoted what I said last year about too much information having been given to the committee; but it was the form in which it was given. He did not go on to say what I had said, that what I was complaining about was the fact that a great deal of this information was not of particular value and served in fact to smother us just as we might be smothered under an avalanche of snow. In this case the avalanche was of paper.
The hon. member for Spadina then went on to say that the work of the committee was not dictated by the Liberal majority on the committee, and that the agenda was drawn up on the basis of suggestions made by the opposition about what should be investigated. Well, the agenda was drawn up all right, but I would point out that at least half of the time of the committee this year was taken up with the Currie report and its appendix. That work was forced on the committee by the vote of the Liberal majority in the house. The Minister of National Defence moved that the first matter to be considered by the committee should be the Currie report. We opposed that just as strongly as we could. We pointed out that if that was done a great deal of the time of the committee would be wasted. We predicted that a major portion of the committee's time would be taken up in threshing
Supply-Defence Production old straw and investigating the investigator whom the government had appointed; that it would be a complete waste of time.
Well, to a large extent our predictions came true. All of the time of the committee was not taken up with it but about one-third of the time was taken up. It was because so much time of the committee was taken up by completely valueless threshing over of the Currie report that we did not have time to go on with very much more important matters dealing with very much larger sums of money. The hon. member for York West and others have complained that we did not get to those matters at all.
I would just like to say a word about what the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Defence Production has had to say about Namao. I do not know whether he actually meant Namao or whether he meant Penhold when he was speaking. He said that charges had been made in connection with the construction at Namao, and I presume he referred to the speech made by the hon. member for Red Deer. That was the only speech to my knowledge in which anything was said by anybody about Namao-before we got into this committee, at any rate.
When the matter came up in the committee the parliamentary assistant said that members could have asked all the questions they wanted about the situation at Namao and could have obtained all the answers, but that not one question was asked. Well, that is a complete misrepresentation of the facts, Mr. Chairman. Nobody on the committee had time to ask many questions about Namao. When Namao first came up we were given some information about why the site was selected and about the type of camp that was to be built there. That information was given by an official of the Department of National Defence, but he had none of the details with regard to the construction which took place, what the member was referring to. He merely gave us information about acquisition of land, the type of camp it was to be, and so on. When questions were asked about construction we were, as usual, referred to the witness from Defence Construction Limited when he should appear or to Mr. Mansur, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing.
Well, Mr. Mansur appeared before the committee for one day, as I remember it. He may have been there a second day when I was not present, but I do not think so. He was just there for one day, and during the day he was there he read a report and answered questions which had been asked at different times previously. There was
4936	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production really no opportunity to question Mr. Mansur to any great extent on any particular project, particularly one such as Namao. The way the agenda was drawn up, when we had Defence Construction Limited before the committee on the last day, the very last day on which we held a full day's session, we had to consider Rocky Point, Esquimalt, one other place and Namao. Questioning went on about Rocky Point and Esquimalt first. About ten minutes before our closing time I began to ask some questions about Namao.
The parliamentary assistant has said that no questions were asked, but that is not correct. I asked what questions I could in the ten minutes available, and that was all the time that was available for asking questions on Namao. As I say, I cite this as just another example of how actual facts in regard to the conduct of the committee are sought to be twisted about and the record snarled by the parliamentary assistant and by the hon. member for Spadina.

Perhaps I should clear that up.
I meant no offence to the hon. member, and my reference was to the appearance before the committee of the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. As a matter of fact I was not present that day, but I looked at the record later and I was very surprised to find that there had been no questions asked of him with respect to the Namao project. I was also surprised that he had not been asked to come back before the committee a second day, because I certainly expected there would be such a volume of questions that he would be required to come back.

The hon. member knows that Mr. Mansur's appearance was immediately before the end of our sitting. We knew we had only one more meeting after that and these various other questions about Rocky Point and other places had already been asked and had to be answered first. In other words, as the agenda was drawn there was no opportunity to bring Mr. Mansur back. It had been decided that he would appear for just the one day.
That was never decided at all.
It was.

In the agenda committee, which was the only meeting of the agenda committee I ever attended, that decision was taken. Well, so much for that particular matter. As I say, I cite it only as an example of how statements are made by representatives of government in this house which give the wrong impression and misrepresent really


what took place. I think the parliamentary assistant has done it through lack of information. He said himself that he was not present at one of those meetings.
I want to say something now about the matter which the hon. member for York West brought up yesterday, the matter of arms production. We spent all of the time this year on the Currie report and the appendix to it, and on construction. The total construction program and everything involved so far as the matter covered by the Currie report was concerned I would say at the most would not involve more than 15 per cent of the total expenditure of some $6 billion on our armament program. I think you could say that, at the best, this year the defence expenditure committee dealt with something in the neighbourhood of 15 per cent or less of the expenditures. We did not deal with the really large expenditures in connection with aircraft production, armaments of all kinds, the training program and other matters along those lines. In my opinion we would have been much better occupied in dealing with those items than in going over some minor accounting irregularities concerning matters scatttered about the country which involved anything from $2.50 up.
This morning I believe the parliamentary assistant said that we had covered those things in great detail last year.
