Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: As far as the position of the hon. member for Melfort is concerned, I am in exactly the same position. A discussion is going on now in the agriculture committee affecting a department for which I am responsible, and I am just as anxious to get there as is the hon. member. If we could make a little progress we could both get there.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Neither of you will get there now.
I was not even insisting; I was leaving it to the chairman. If the minister wants to challenge me, I am prepared to stay and see that he stays here as well.
Carried, carried.

There is an old adage which says that a little fellow spirit makes us wondrous kind. I feel very kindly toward the leader of the government and the minister at the present time, because during the debates of the committee considering defence expenditure, I sat through hours and hours and hours of questioning which I thought was as aimless as the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Skeena.
I am not at all surprised that the minister is rather anxious to get on with the estimates. I was anxious to get on with the discussion of some of the important matters in connection with defence expenditure; but I am loath to let this item pass until I receive a reply to the questions I asked the minister yesterday regarding the production of naval vessels and the reason there is a delay in the production of those naval vessels. I also asked particularly about the distribution of some of the contracts to the Pacific coast. I do not want to have hon. members say "carried, carried" until I get a reply to those questions. They are very definitely connected with this item and I feel I am entitled to have them answered, and I do not want any of this "carried, carried" business.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have been trying to break through the smokescreen to answer the hon. member's questions for the last 24 hours, but the smoke has been too dense.
And I have been patiently waiting for the answers.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
With respect to subsidies for shipyards, there are no subsidies for any shipyards in Canada. Certain capital assistance has been given for equipment required for the naval program and not reasonably required for the ordinary work of a shipyard. That assistance, however, has been in small

Supply-Defence Production amounts and pretty well distributed among major shipyards.
The distribution of ship construction or repair work has been worked out by the maritime commission to a large extent. It is the policy of the commission to keep the principal shipyards active and have them in a position where they could undertake an expanded program of naval construction without undue delay. There is an attempt to have in every shipyard trained men who could handle that class of work. The principal program has been escort vessels and that work has been assigned to the west coast rather out of proportion to the distribution to the eastern yards. It was thought that the program could be very well carried on out west. Five of the fourteen escort vessels have been assigned to the west coast, and the conversion of two destroyers into escort vessels has also been scheduled for that area.
We accept the direction of the maritime commission with respect to distribution. It was established some years ago that naval work not subject to tender would be allocated by the maritime commission, and that policy has been followed.
With respect to castings, the lead yard has been responsible for securing items common to all escort vessels or vessels of a certain type. Procurement is worked out by the lead yard in consultation with our own director of shipbuilding and a representative of the navy. How much of that lead yard work has been carried out on the west coast I do not know. Some rather important equipment installations have been carried out on the west coast. One rather important segment was placed with Vivian Engines, but I do not remember just what item of naval equipment it was. I think other items have been placed on the west coast, but there again the needs of the program must have prior importance to the geographical distribution. It is just impossible to distribute highly specialized naval work across Canada in a way that disregards cost and disregards equipment available in plants.
Have I answered the question?
Yes, but perhaps I might ask a supplementary question. You referred to the lead yard in respect of castings. Where would that lead yard be?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The lead yard for the escort program is Canadian Vickers in Montreal. The lead yard draws on the designing talent of all yards for the particular program, and it was felt that the situation in Montreal was more convenient than in any other yard associated with that program. I believe that Davie

is the lead yard for another type of vessel, minesweepers. Just who the other lead yards are for other types of vessels, I am not sure.

I do not want to prolong the discussion, but would it not be possible to have these castings made in foundries on the west coast where ships are being constructed, and where there has been delay in the completion of ships because castings have to be sent from eastern Canada? Delay has been caused and, very often, there have been lay-offs of key personnel. I am informed, and I believe correctly, that some of these key personnel have left the country and gone to United States shipyards because of the greater certainty of being steadily employed there. It seems to me that the production of *castings for certain of this equipment, where the facilities do exist on the west coast, might have been possible in the past, and it may still be possible to allocate that work to the west coast yards to ensure continuance of work there and retention of the key mechanics who are so essential for our shipbuilding industry on the west coast.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the theory behind having the lead yard do the purchasing of castings for all fourteen escort ships is that there are so few pieces produced that it does not pay to duplicate the moulds. These are rather intricate castings. That is the theory behind it, anyway; whether it is sound in the case of the castings referred to by my hon. friend I do not know. Apparently, in the judgment of those responsible, it was the wise thing to have the castings made in the one foundry. It brings about the elimination of duplicate moulds for the one casting.
All I ask is that the situation be reviewed; because it seems to me there are other arguments which could be advanced for having particular work carried out on the west coast.

I have a few questions with regard to Canadian Commercial Corporation, which is specifically mentioned in item 79. I take it that this is the proper place to discuss that corporation. I want to ask the minister to bring us up to date with regard to the Canadian Commercial Corporation. I want to refer very briefly to its inception, io the change which has taken place in its functions over the years, and then to ask the minister where we stand now.
I want to recall to the committee that we have five organizations: the Department of National Defence, the Department of Defence Production, Defence Construction Limited,

Canadian Commercial Corporation and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I want to recall that Canadian Commercial Corporation was set up in 1946. Apparently it had three chief functions at that time, and I am reading from page 3191 of Hansard for July 5, 1946, where the minister of trade and commerce of those days, Mr. MacKinnon, said:
-the Canadian Commercial Corporation will be called upon to discharge . . . the work hitherto performed by the Canadian export board which made purchases in Canada for foreign governments . . .
Then on the next page he said:
The corporation will not encroach upon the activities of private business; in fact one of its primary objectives will be to assist it directly in many important ways. For example, in the import field, it will aid Canadian traders in obtaining essential supplies from ex-enemy territories under military occupation.
On the next page he said:
The Canadian Commercial Corporation also will provide a means which, if desirable, can be used, in the future, for purchasing commodities under international allocation or foreign government control such as sugar, tea-*
And so on. At that time Mr. MacKinnon said it was contemplated the corporation would just last for what he called the transitional period. When he was asked what that might be, he said two or three years. I appreciate fully that the situation changed after that.
I am going to read a sentence from a speech by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in 1951, at the time the defence production department was set up. By that time I understand the functions of the Canadian Commercial Corporation were considerably changed; they had also changed in the interval. I read a sentence from what the minister said to show what the nature of the change was, and what the Canadian Commercial Corporation was doing in 1951, at the time the defence production department was set up. I read from page 838 of Hansard for March 2, 1951, where the minister said:
The Canadian Commercial Corporation now acts as an agent of the minister in carrying out procurement of the requirements of the three services.
Then he went on:
With a separate department of defence production, the general purchasing would be carried out as a direct function of the department-
That is the Department of Defence Production.
-and the great majority of the staff of the Canadian Commercial Corporation would be transferred to the department for that purpose.
Then the minister went on to say, on the same page:
It is not proposed, however, to wind up the corporation as such, but rather to retain it as a
Supply-Defence Production special agency to handle transactions with other governments or to engage in the bulk purchasing or stockpiling of any defence supplies or strategic materials which may be necessary.
Then the minister added:
The corporation, with such terms of reference, would probably fulfil a role not dissimilar to that filled by War Supplies Limited during the last war.
In that connection I want to read just one sentence describing the function of War Supplies Limited, which I am reading from the "History of the Department of Munitions and Supply" at page 478, the last paragraph:
War Supplies Limited fulfilled the very important function of co-ordinating the fiscal system of Canada and the United States, and also was an important factor in enabling Canada to maintain control of materials, industry and labour during the war years.
I imagine when the minister made that statement it was a general reference, and I am not pursuing it. I want now to come to this:	I am not quite clear on the importance of the functions now being carried out by the Canadian Commercial Corporation. I think I understand what Defence Construction does, and its separate function. I understand what Central Mortgage and Housing does, and its separate function. But it is not clear to me what important separate function the Canadian Commercial Corporation discharges.
Before I take my seat, and before the minister answers that, I want to ask this question, too. I have here a report of the Canadian Commercial Corporation for the period April 1, 1951 to March 31, 1952; that is more than a year old. I hope the minister will be able to bring us up to date on that so we will know the nature of the operations of the Canadian Commercial Corporation within the last year. In particular, I should like to know the nature of its operations in connection with the acquisition of materials, and what there is on hand at the present time. I observe that under the general account, as it is called in this statement of April, 1951, the inventory of commodities on hand is only $413,000. Now, I realize that a good many of the commodities on hand may be carried in corporations other than the Canadian Commercial Corporation which, I take it, acts as agent. I should be glad if the minister would answer those questions.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Perhaps we had better start at the beginning, since the hon. member has covered a good deal of territory. In the early days of the second world war we were doing a good deal of business with Washington, and Washington wanted to deal with the Canadian government through a corporate entity located in the city of Washington. At that time we formed a crown company,

Supply-Defence Production War Supplies Limited, with a head office in Washington, D.C., which accepted all orders placed by the government of the United States and forwarded them to Ottawa. This organization was responsible for their execution, so far as the United States government was concerned, and it was the one point of contact for any procurement on behalf of the United States government or on behalf of any other foreign governments. There were several foreign governments operating from Washington or New York at the time, and all foreign business was placed through War Supplies Limited.
After the war ended and after the outstanding contracts had been completed, there seemed to be no further purpose in continuing War Supplies Limited, so the company was wound up. However, the then minister of trade and commerce, the Hon. Mr. MacKinnon, felt the need for an organization in his department to handle foreign business. He was bringing in a good deal of material from countries that could not trade directly with Canada, and he formed the Canadian Commercial Corporation to carry out the foreign business, both buying for Canadian account and selling Canadian goods to foreign governments. It was used largely for the latter purpose. Governments abroad that wished to buy in Canada bought through the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
During this period, it was thought advisable to wind up the department of munitions and supply. It was felt that the department, which was represented in every city from coast to coast, had an overhead greater than the volume of the purchasing it was called upon to do would warrant. The department was, therefore, wound up and the functions of the department were transferred to the Canadian Commercial Corporation under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. For a period the Canadian Commercial Corporation handled the principal functions now being administered by the Department of Defence Production.
When the preparedness program was undertaken, it was found that the corporation was getting too unwieldy and that the corporate set-up was no longer suitable, so the Department of Defence Production was organized. This department has taken over all the responsibilities for Department of National Defence procurement from the Canadian Commercial Corporation. Today the Canadian Commercial Corporation is doing exactly what War Supplies Limited did in the last war. It accepts orders from foreign governments and places them through this department in Canada. It has placed


something over $300 million worth of orders from the government of the United States. It has handled business from other governments that wished to place orders in Canada through the Department of Defence Production. It also handles purchasing for the Colombo plan and the shipment of goods to Colombo plan destinations.

I want to have an idea of the magnitude of the operation. I observe from, this report that the total supply of Canadian goods and commodities of governments and international organizations handled through the corporation during the fiscal year, that is the fiscal year ended March 31, 1952, was $206 million. Could the minister give me a roughly corresponding figure for the last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I should think the total today is something over $400 million. I am sorry that the report corresponding to the one my hon. friend has read from is not yet prepared, but we have not been able to get the services of the Auditor General to audit the books. Therefore we have not been able to table it in the house. I think probably during the past year the Canadian Commercial Corporation placed orders for another $200 million.
As to the stockpiling of strategic materials, I might say that the purchasing is handled through the Canadian Commercial Corporation but the actual stockpiling is financed through the revolving fund of which my hon. friend has such great knowledge.
I remember the revolving fund. That is to say, the stuff in the stockpile is carried by defence production?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The stockpiling of strategic materials such as tin, quartz crystals and one or two other metals is carried by the department through the revolving fund.

I have one other question. I observe here in the general account some $19 million of advances to suppliers which I understand are for progress payments. I am recalling the unfortunate advances we made to the Davie company in 1949, when we sustained a bit of a loss. What is the practice in making advances to suppliers? What I mean is this. Are these all substantial people of ascertained position? Have we made any losses other than the George T. Davie loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No. A good deal has been said about the George T. Davie loss. My hon. friend will recall that all the details of the transaction were explained to parliament at the time, and at least the tacit approval of

parliament was obtained before the transaction was completed.

The information the minister gave me a few minutes ago is not the complete answer to the question I asked last night. I had asked him to bring us up to date with regard to the progress of the shipbuilding program and the reasons for the delays or the lag in the program. I understand that there is a considerable lag behind the anticipated production. It is stated in the report:
The launching of a bare hull represents only some 3 per cent of the total man hours required to complete a destroyer escort for sea duty.
I realize that, but I should like to know how near we are to commissioning these various vessels which are now being constructed or being completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The conversions are coming along well. I think all the conversions of frigates and Bangors will be completed during the current year. We were too optimistic about the time required from the drafting board to completion of the escort vessels. We are wiser now. Britain has been carrying on a somewhat similar program, and it has taken over six years from the time the drafting work was first undertaken to completion of the first escort vessel. In the United States it has taken a little over five years for a similar program. In Canada it will be about five and a half years before the program is completed.
Five and a half years from now?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Five and a half years; yes.
From now?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No. From the time the work was first put on the drafting board.
That was 1951?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: 1951. It will be 1956 before the program is completed. No, it was put on the drafting board before that. It was undertaken in 1949. The first destroyers will be delivered to the navy complete during 1954. Whether they will all be delivered in 1954 is not so certain. Some of them may go over into 1955.
Is there any truth in the story that men and materials have been diverted to work on freighters for foreign countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No. That is not true. The difficulty has been in getting sufficient designers and draftsmen to keep the design work ahead of production. We have taken quite extraordinary steps in that connection. We have brought men from the United States and we have brought a number of men from England. Of course each country's naval program is at its peak now, and it is extremely difficult to
Supply-Defence Production get men. But that problem is fairly well over. Our design work is now well up to date. Subcontracts are going well. Today it is simply a matter of putting on maximum manpower and getting the work finished.
This is the last question I have. What about the minesweeper program? There have been delays.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Minesweepers?
Yes, minesweepers. There has not been the same technical detail there.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.
There seem to have been delays.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We hoped to get some of those last year. Ten of them will be delivered during the current fiscal year.
None have been delivered yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No. The first goes on trial very shortly.

I should like to ask the minister a question. I come from a town which is known as a great shipyard town, namely Collingwood, Ontario. We have been extremely fortunate there in the past six years in making vessels for private enterprise. At the present time, owing to the extension of the pipe line, 400 men have been laid off at the shipyard that is noted across Canada for its efficiency and its capability. Does the minister believe some naval vessels may be constructed on the great lakes, or that there are some it is possible to construct on the great lakes, in order to make them of value to this country? I should like to know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Of course the situation at Collingwood is the result of a little bit of bad luck.
I know that.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Work was suspended on the vessel that is under way. Arrangements have now been made to complete the vessel as a grain carrier. I believe some delay was caused through revising the design. Whether there will be other work for that yard we are not certain. I understand that there is some further naval work in contemplation. If that is the case, I am sure the maritime commission will keep in mind the Collingwood yard.
I greatly appreciate what the minister has said. I am sure he knows, from the speech he made in Collingwood prior to the 1949 election-

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
They didn't believe me.
4958	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production
-that they are extremely capable people. He assured the people of my community at that time that he would not neglect Collingwood. I hope he lives up to his promise.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: They did not vote right.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Collingwood yard has been an extra busy yard. No one believed me before. They will not believe me if I go back.
They will take you for what you are worth this time, I am sure, the same as they did the last time.
I am coming back to the question I asked before and which I hope will be more convenient under this item. I refer to the amount of strategic materials which have been purchased and which are on hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not think we should give that information. The United States has consistently refused to give the size of their strategic stockpile. I should be glad to give it to my hon. friend privately, but I am sure he would not want me to put it on the record.

I shall not press that question. My final question is this. I think I can understand why Defence Construction Limited was necessary as an adjunct or an agent of defence production; because of its technical nature, it needs technical men. I can quite see that defence production did not want to staff itself in that way. But it is not clear to me why defence production needs in addition Canadian Commercial Corporation, which seems to me now to have been altered so completely. Indeed, it has been twice altered in its nature. It began, as was mentioned in Mr. MacKinnon's speech, six years ago. It then became agent for procurement for the services. Now it is changed again. It is not yet clear to me why we need able men-I am referring now to the civil servants-doing this job, and I am wondering whether it could not be done equally well by defence production itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The reason is that foreign governments like to be able to deal with a corporate entity. It is much easier for a corporation to sign the documentation necessary to complete a purchase by a foreign government than it is for the government of Canada to do so. The government of Canada would require special order in council authority and a good deal of extra documentation, thus it would take much more time.


The Canadian Commercial Corporation has gone the full cycle; it is doing exactly the work that its predecessor, War Supplies Limited, did in the last war. Just as War Supplies Limited was a very necessary tool in that war, so I believe the Canadian Commercial Corporation is a very necessary tool in the present defence program. To date it has entered into contracts totalling $456 million.

Is that
cumulative?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, that is since April 1, 1951. It has a staff of about 40 people, an office in Washington and headquarters in Ottawa.
The minister's reference to an order in council has called up one other question to my mind. What is the authority for the order in council mentioned on page 11 in the minister's report?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is a regulation under the Financial Administration Act. The Financial Administration Act was passed by this house within the last twelve months. It provided for regulations, and the order in council in question was passed under that act.

I have two questions only to put to the minister. I have been very patient, sitting here all day, and I hope the minister will be patient with me. I have a return from the Department of Defence Production in reply to the following questions:
1.	What defence projects are presently being undertaken in Newfoundland by the Department of National Defence?
2.	Where are they located?
3.	What is the estimated cost of each project?
I received details showing that in St. John's, Newfoundland, there was one of $680,600; one in Goose Bay, Labrador, $6,622,078, and another one in Goose Bay, Labrador, $174,500. If I am still able to add correctly, that makes a total of $7,477,178. The question I am asking is this. In the budget speech of the minister of finance of Newfoundland, delivered on April 29, he estimated the moneys that would be going into the pockets of the people of Newfoundland in 1953, and he set forth a table in which he gave the amounts for defence in 1951, 1952 and what they would earn in 1953. In 1951 he said the total was $16 million; in 1952, $21,989,000 and in 1953, $24,533,000.
If we take the $24,533,000 the provincial minister says is to be earned this year in Newfoundland and subtract from it the $7,477,178 that the return given me today shows, it leaves a balance of $17,055,822, if my subtraction is correct.

I want to ask the minister this question. Does the return I hold in my hand represent all that is being spent for defence in Newfoundland, or is the balance of $17 million odd being spent entirely by the United States?

The $7 million odd represents the amount being spent by our department in Newfoundland, pay and allowances of the troops and expenditures by other departments of government. However, I have discussed this matter with the members of the government of Newfoundland. The whole point is that they are so busy looking after the work that is closer at home that they are not very anxious to get our work. They admit it quite frankly. In fact the premier told me only a few days ago that to carry out the work in sight for this summer, men would have to be brought in from outside the province. Therefore I suggest that the department can hardly be blamed if the province finds itself in that position.

That is not quite the answer, Mr. Chairman, with all due respect. I am not in any way disputing the minister's answer, but the question I am putting is this: Is the total amount of work he would have done this year, no matter who does it, $7,477,000 as I got it in the return today? That is correct, I presume.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: By our department, yes.
No other department is doing work there that I know of.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Department of Transport is doing work there, and the Department of National Defence is certainly making very considerable expenditures through the Department of Defence Production as indicated by the amount given in the return, but those are by no means all the expenditures of this government in Newfoundland.

I certainly do not want to take the minister to task in any way, but the questions I put and to which I have a return are these. There were five questions. The first was:
What defence projects are presently being undertaken in Newfoundland by the Department of National Defence?
They give me all the projects, setting them forth by departments, and after that they tell me the amounts, and then the grand total. Remember, this includes not only the profits on contracts, but all the people who are supplying the contracts are mentioned, and this includes the money that the ordinary labourer is making. The minister of finance of Newfoundland said that the take-home pay of the people working on these contracts was going to be $24,533,000. I merely ask
Supply-Defence Production if there is more work going on down there than we know or the minister knows, or is this work being done by the United States forces?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is United States contracts.

That is fine. My second question is in connection with the defence orders that I have been asking about for some time now at the new machinery plant, and I am certainly not going to be nasty about this. Last November I asked the parliamentary assistant to tell the minister that I was going to ask a question as to the prospects of orders for that plant. That went on for a matter of two months, and ultimately the parliamentary assistant suggested that I should put the question on the order paper. I put the question on the order paper on December 12, 1952. I am going to read the question and answer. They are not very long. They are as follows:
1.	Have any orders for the supply of defence materials been given the new machinery plant at Topsail Road, Newfoundland?
2.	If so, what orders have been given, and what has been the value of such orders?
3.	If not, is it intended that any orders will be given and when may the same be expected?
On January 14, 1953 they were answered as follows:
1.	No defence orders have as yet been placed with Canadian Machinery and Industry Construction Limited, by the Department of Defence Production.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	Their facilities are well known to officials of the Department of Defence Production. The company is receiving all appropriate invitations to tender and the department is also examining the possibility of placing a specialized contract in this plant.
On March 6 I placed these questions on the order paper:
1.	Has the Department of Defence Production placed any orders with the new machinery plant at Topsail Road, Newfoundland, for the supply of defence material?
2.	Has the placing of a specialized contract for this plant been considered, and, if so, what is the result of such consideration?
These questions were answered as follows:
1.	No.
2.	Yes. No orders materialized.
I now have a question on the order paper asking if there are any possibilities of orders. All I ask the minister is this: Is there any future outlook for defence orders for that plant? I think the minister knows I am not trying to bulldoze him, but we are getting anxious about the future of that plant.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not know that my hon. friend need be so anxious. The plant is doing well. In respect to the prospects of future orders, I may say we were trying to work out a military order for it, but we found

Supply-Defence Production that the plant did not have the capacity to take it, without a new building. The cost of that addition would have put the overhead on the order we were trying to place with the company at a prohibitive level.
However, I am told that the plant is doing well. It is getting all the work on the island of Newfoundland; and if we have any work there satisfactory for the plant, we will place it with them. If the company cares to tender on work on the mainland we shall be glad to consider their tender. I think my hon. friend is distressing himself unduly in the matter.

I thought the minister said the plant was getting all the orders on the island of Newfoundland. Well, that may be so; but there are not many orders there. The plant is practically idle. I have looked through the public accounts and I find that a tremendous number of small machinery plants are getting orders. All I am asking is whether there is going to be an order for that plant.
Carried.

No. I have something further to say; perhaps it would almost amount to a point of order. This afternoon the chairman of the defence expenditure committee brought up the point that in the committee because I had not asked specific questions dealing with aircraft production, therefore I had not brought that matter before the committee.
In that connection I would draw the attention of hon. members to the report appearing in Hansard of January 16 where, as reported at page 1076, on the occasion of setting up the committee, I said:
I feel that no parliament can divest itself of the responsibility for national defence. The old days of the professional soldier are over. Today every citizen is part of the defence of his country, and the better he is informed the more effective he can be. These basic problems therefore must be discussed and studied.
I suggest that men like Air Marshal Douglas Smith, the air member for technical services, with his engine and airplane specialists, and Dr. J. J. Green, as well as Dr. Solandt, could most profitably come before the committee.
And subsequently that day:
I earnestly hope that when the committee is set up the terms of reference will be broadened so we will know not only that the money being expended is adequately and properly expended, but that it results in fighting material which will be useful and effective. If we do not do that we are not only negligent in our duty, but it may almost be said that we are traitors to our cause.
Well, the chairman of the committee, in discussing aircraft production, the subject to which I referred last night-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. This afternoon when the chairman of the defence expenditure

committee, the hon. member for Spadina, was making the point that the hon. member for York West had not asked questions in the committee about aircraft production, I understood the hon. member for York West to rise and clarify the position. I allowed him this evening to make the quotation in order to support the point he made this afternoon. But I would suggest to him that certainly we are not going back to what took place this afternoon, or earlier this morning.

It is not my intention to go back to what was done this afternoon. It is merely my intention to clarify what was said about aircraft production. And in view of the minister's statement on February 16 with regard to the production of jet aircraft, in which he specifically referred to the hon. memher for Kamloops and myself as being two of the reasons for making the statement,
I would say that this was a most important problem with which the minister had dealt, but that certain doubts were left in our minds in connection with the production of modern aircraft.
The minister said, I believe it was on February 16, that he could not proceed to discuss the matter because of the question of security. Well, subsequent to that a considerable amount of what people who seem to know tell me amounts to breaches of security, appeared in the government press. Perhaps it was just a case of zealous reporting, perhaps it was not. I happen to know a certain amount about what went on.
However, I feel most sincerely that it was the duty of the defence expenditure committee to go into these matters and hear from the experts who knew the meaning of security, who could say, "Thus far we can go; beyond that would be a breach of security." We could have heard from men who knew the subject, not from members of a political party. We could have heard from men who have the job of fighting, and of defending the country.
That was my point last night. That is my point tonight. And, with respect, that is the point which has been completely distorted by the chairman of the defence committee. I think it would have been extremely helpful to hon. members and to the country to have had before the committee persons such as I have suggested.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would ask the hon. member to come to those matters which really fall under the jurisdiction of the Department of Defence Production, and I would ask him not to refer again to what took place in the committee on defence expenditure. There has

been some discussion on that point. I thought it had been concluded.
I have only one sentence more-and may I say I agree entirely with you, Mr. Chairman. The question has been debated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I point out to the hon. member that he also agreed with me when I rose earlier.

Yes, I did; but I qualified my agreement by stating that we have to have the complete data straightened out in the house, and that the whole question of aircraft production is one which is definitely a problem of the Department of Defence Production. It is almost a primary problem in defence production, I suggest, and it is one which should not be dealt with in the heat of political debate, in the heat of controversy. I do not include you in that, Mr. Chairman, but refer to debate across the floor of the house. The information should come from an expert level. That, it seems to me, summarizes the failure, and indicates what we have not done at this session in reviewing defence production.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
This afternoon I asked the minister several questions regarding arms production, particularly in respect of the production of cannon, small arms and ammunition. Can he answer those questions now?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes. My hon. friend would not expect me, of course, to give the numbers and deliveries of guns. He knows that is classified material. However, I would be pleased to give a general outline.
Prime contracts for guns are almost completely placed with Canadian Arsenals, who operate on a straight cost basis, without profit. In placing subcontracts, Canadian Arsenals attempt to get fixed prices as a result of competitive tenders. The one important exception to the above is Sorel Industries Limited which has been chosen by both the Canadian and United States governments as a producer of larger calibre weapons. In these contracts we are working toward target price contracts as we secure cost information.
The principal weapons include the 3-inch 50 calibre now being delivered to the United States in accordance with their requirement schedule. The 120 mm. gun for the United States army is now coming into production and deliveries will commence within a few weeks. Sorel Industries will also manufacture the 105 mm. recoilless rifle. No production has yet started because the weapon is being redesigned in the United States. This plant will also produce the 40 mm.
Supply-Defence Production Bofors for the Canadian navy. Deliveries on this item are to begin early in 1954.
The Arsenals are now producing the -5" Browning machine gun for the CF-100 and the F-86 Sabre. 60 mm. and 81 mm. mortars will be produced by the Turnbull Elevator Company, Toronto, and Vivian Engine Works, Vancouver. Deliveries of the 3-5" rocket launcher are now practically completed by the Firestone Tire and Rubber Company and Canadian Arsenals. Apart from secret experimental work there is no production of small arms for Canadian account at this time.
Information was wanted about ammunition. For all gun ammunition, cartridge cases are being produced by Canadian Arsenals at Quebec city. The ammunition is filled at the arsenal filling plant at St. Paul l'Ermite. It is not appropriate to discuss details of ammunition production schedules due to security implications. It should be noted that our troops in Korea are receiving their ammunition through United States supply channels and not directly from Canada. However, we are making some contribution from our production facilities, both to the United States and United Kingdom forces.
Among the important types of ammunition now being delivered or coming into production are the following:
155 mm. shell; forging and machining by Canadian Car and Foundry; some deliveries already made.
105 mm. shell; forging by National Steel Car, Hamilton, Ontario; deliveries to begin in about a month.
90 mm. shell; forging and machining by Trenton Steel Company, Trenton, Nova Scotia; deliveries are being made at the present time.
3" 50 calibre rounds; order for forgings by Dominion Forge and Stamping completed. '
40 mm. Bofors rounds; machining by Arsenals; deliveries under way .
60 mm. mortar bombs; forging and machining by Thompson Products Limited; deliveries to begin in a few months.
81 mm. mortar bombs; forging and machining by Massey-Harris; deliveries of the body only have begun.
[DOT]50 machine gun rounds; Canadian Arsenals; deliveries under way.
Bombs, practice, 100 pounds; by Modern Moulding and Metal Craft; order almost completed.
Bombs, practice, 25 pounds; Sorel Industries Limited; deliveries under way.
Hand grenades No. 83; T. W. Hand Fireworks Company Limited; order almost completed.

Supply-Defence Production
Rocket, 3-5" head, by Orillia Sheet Metal; motor body assembly by Moffatt's Limited, and fuse by Wallaceburg Brass; deliveries have begun.
Rockets, aircraft, 2-25"; metal parts by Firestone Tire and Rubber Company, Hamilton; deliveries almost completed.

I did not notice any 25-
pounder gun ammunition being manufactured. The 25-pounder is the gun used by our forces in Korea. Are we supplying any of that ammunition or are we depending on British sources?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We sent substantial quantities of 25-pounder ammunition to the United Kingdom, but our artillery there is on the British supply line and the replacements are coming from the United Kingdom. We explored the desirability of manufacturing more 25-pounder ammunition, but the joint decision was against our doing so.
Did the minister mention anything about the production of guided missiles?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.
That is completely classified at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes. It might be interesting to note the point of view taken in the British parliament, and I quote the following:
D. P. T. Jay asked the minister of supply the total ot public money spent by his department on aircraft research and development undertaken by aircraft companies since April, 1945. The minister replied: "It would not be in the public interest to give information about government expenditure on aeronautical research and development, the overwhelming majority of which is for military types".
Are the snowmobiles purchased by the department proving satisfactory and practical under northern Canadian conditions?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The trials have been entirely satisfactory. I understand that in the northern exercises the Canadian snowmobile stood up whereas the snowmobile furnished from south of the line did not.
Are they all produced by the one company?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am not sure. I was under the impression that there were two suppliers, but I do not know who the other one is.
Are the items in stock now all serviceable and in working order?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Serviceability is a matter for the Department of National Defence. We would not know that; we just buy them.
How many hundreds of thousands of navy hat bands have been bought-
Oh, oh.
Oh, oh. You can "oh, oh" all you like. The "oh, oh's" are from the Liberal benches. I want to know how many were bought from agents in Canada who in turn bought them from western Germany.
None.
Now you are wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: How many times does my hon. friend require an answer to that question. We answered it in writing. I cannot remember the answer.
I have not had it in writing.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We certainly have had it in the house. It was either a written return or it is on Hansard. I wish I could remember figures like that as long as they are required, but I cannot.
I want to know how many that were bought were made in Germany.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I could not tell you.
I know there were at least 200,000, and I just wondered how many more.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is the difference; my hon. friend knows the answer and I do not.
I want to know how many more than that.
Funny if it has been answered several times and you do not know the answer.
Cannot the minister state how many hundreds of thousands were bought from Germany?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The minister has said he does not know. Perhaps the answer is being looked up. In the meantime we could carry on the discussion.

There are several individual points on which I should like to have information or explanation. The first has to do with the last question asked by the hon. member for Greenwood in connection with order in council P.C. 3209 of May 30, 1952, which is referred to at the bottom of page 11 of the annual report of the department. The effect of that order in council, which was passed under section 39 of the Financial Administration Act, requires, as is indicated in the report, reference to and approval by the treasury board in the case of orders for amounts between $25,000 and $50,000. I should like to ask the minister if that approval of treasury board has been treated as a substitute for approval by the governor in council?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, it has. Provision for that was made in the act which was passed by this parliament. Orders in council of that type were formerly passed by a committee of the privy council. The Financial Administration Act made provision for the work to be carried out in future by the treasury board, which is also a committee of the privy council with pretty much the same membership. It is not an important change. There is a larger and better staff for vetting orders than the privy council had.

What has been the practice of the department with respect to placing orders within that price range without tender? I asked the minister last night if he would make a statement concerning the practice of the department with respect to calling for tenders in the case of orders, first of all, in the category up to $25,000 and, second, in the category from $25,000 to $50,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The practice universally is to call for tenders except, for example, if we are buying parts for a Ford car. We would not call for tenders there, but we would go to the manufacturer and buy them under a contract with the manufacturer. I would say that except for purchases of that type, where there is proprietary interest involved and where tenders would not be productive of any saving, everything bought by the department under $50,000 is bought by tender.

The next point I have to raise is one I brought up when the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were before us, and he asked that it be deferred until the estimates of this department were before the committee. It relates to a report which appears in a press dispatch of August 14 last purporting to contain.a statement by the minister that this country was making a gift of arms to the value of $150 million to the United Kingdom in 1952. In the Canadian Press dispatch from London the following day it was indicated that the authorities over there were consulting in regard to the matter. The dispatch indicates that a treasury spokesman said:
[DOT]-the figure of $150 million announced by Howe was "a new figure here hut we believe Mr. Howe was misreported in saying that it would all be spendable this year."
Then the dispatch proceeds to indicate that the talk must have been in relation to the commitments undertaken at the Lisbon conference of the NATO organization, but they were not too clear about how the amount was arrived at. I wonder if the minister would make a full statement to the committee.
Supply-Defence Production

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
That report was unfortunate. The figure of $150 million was right, but I did not say that it would be expended in one year. I was just going into the building when a reporter asked me to comment on a dispatch published in the Manchester Guardian, to the effect that Canada was indifferent. Actually the expression was "Olympian detachment". I said I did not know that Canada was so detached because we were providing Britain with some $150 million worth of aid. That was all I said, and I walked into the building. The reporter built a full column around that remark, and it caused some repercussions.
The fact was that in the fiscal year which he put in the story, but which I did not, we provided the United Kingdom with about $130 million worth of mutual aid. During that fiscal year the items were largely F-86 airframes, mark IV No. 6 radar sets, picrite and other explosives. Since then we have sent very much more, so the $150 million was quite safe at that time. The figure also includes the air training program.
May I ask what period of time the $150 million covers?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not know the cut-off date exactly, but I know that we are sending military aid to Britain. We send military aid to NATO and it is allocated by NATO to Britain; but we are sending direct allocations to Britain in the form of material and expenditures for air training well in excess of $150 million at the present time. Perhaps the figure is nearer $200 million now.
Then I take it that the $150 million does not relate to any specified period.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No, although the dispatch
referred to one year.
It said "this year", apparently indicating 1952.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Our expenditures were about $130 million for the year, but for the full period they are considerably more than that.

The other question I have relates to the purchase of gloves. If the minister has not the information now perhaps he could have one of his officials communicate it to me. I gave the figures last night on the purchase of gloves and mitts, based on a return from the department, to December 31, 1952. They appear in Hansard on page 4878. What purchases of gloves or mitts have been made since January 1, 1953, or have been ordered since that date?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I would be glad to look into that.

I have a question I would like to ask the minister. Perhaps he made

Supply-Defence Production reference to it this afternoon, but as I was in committee I did not have a chance to hear whether he made any comment on it at all. I refer to restrictions on steel, and I would like to ask if there are any limitations in effect on the distribution of certain types of steel. If there are limitations, is it possible that they may be completely removed in the near future?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There are practically no restrictions on steel. We reserve the right to call for end user certificates. In other words, if a large order is being placed we get a certificate indicating the end use to which the steel is allocated. We keep that measure in force so that if another steel shortage develops we will have machinery to allocate or direct steel to defence projects. Today steel is not difficult to buy and there are practically no restrictions on its purchase by anyone. We do, however, keep tighter control of steel scrap.

I would like to ask a question about Sorel Industries Limited, but if we are still giving capital assistance to that company I could ask it under the next item. Would the minister say whether we are still providing capital assistance to that company?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes, there is still capital assistance being provided there. We have several contracts with them, and the capital assistance is being carried on.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
80. To provide capital assistance for the construction, acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works by private contractors engaged in defence contracts, or by crown plants operated on a management-fee basis, or by crown companies under direction of the Minister of Defence Production, subject to approval of treasury board, $60,000,000.

I notice that this item is to provide capital assistance for the construction, acquisition, extension or improvement of capital equipment or works by private contractors. Of course we are all vitally interested in this, and I would like to ask the minister just what capital assistance is being given in the different provinces in Canada. I am particularly interested in my own province of New Brunswick.
I might say we are very proud indeed to have the minister as a summer resident of our province, and he is very much interested in the development down there. However, I would like to ask the minister just what capital assistance has been given under this item to concerns in the province of New Brunswick and in other provinces. I notice that the amount was $110 million last year and it has


been reduced to $60 million this year, a reduction of $50 million. Could the minister give a breakdown of the amounts?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have no breakdown by provinces. We are not interested in a provincial breakdown; we are interested in buying material. We are not running a political shop, and we do not divide the figures into political entities.

I am not asking this from a political point of view, but I am interested in my province and I should think the minister would be interested in developing industry in the province of New Brunswick. For instance, one reads every few weeks a list of the purchases that are made throughout Canada. One sees that so much oil was purchased, or so much was purchased from the Swift Company in our province, and so on. However, I had not read anything which said that very much had been given to industry in that province.
We talk about decentralization, and so on. If we are going to decentralize industry, it does seem to me the minister should be interested in giving assistance to the development of industry in the province. I do not see why his officials who are sitting in front of him cannot tell us what assistance has been given in the different provinces so far as this item is concerned. They must have a breakdown of it, and I should like the minister to give us that breakdown.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have no breakdown by provinces. If the hon. member will ask me whether or not any particular firm in the province has received capital assistance, I shall be able to tell him. We are buying from industry where there is industry. For instance, I live in the -town of St. Andrews, New Brunswick, and I should like very much to buy war materials from that place but they do not make them. On the other hand, in Saint John we do buy a good deal from the Saint John Dry Dock Company and one or two other firms there. We have extended capital assistance in Saint John, and I wish I could tell him that the same was true in every town in New Brunswick, but I cannot. I do not carry those things in my head, and there is no purpose in the department attempting to break the thing down by provinces, by constituencies, or by towns and villages.

I do not see why the minister cannot give us a list of the industries in New Brunswick which are receiving assistance from his department. We have heard a lot in this house about decentralization of

industry. It does seem to me that the minister is very much interested in the decentralization of industry. If we are decentralizing industry, surely he must know something about the different industries in the different provinces that have received assistance from his department. If he cannot give me the information now, I should like to receive the information later.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I can say this, that we have not refused capital assistance to any industry in New Brunswick which has applied for it and where it was justified. I do not think I can go farther than that, but my officers confirm that fact.
Possibly we might know what percentage of industry in the maritimes has received assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I have not the faintest idea.
I am satisfied that it is very small.

I have several questions concerning capital assistance. I received a return on March 2, 1953 which showed that capital assistance had been received by the A. V. Roe Company for the development of the Orenda engine in the amount of $52 million, and for the CF-100 airframe in the amount of $11 million. I am leaving off the hundreds of thousands. Another return also received on March 2 showed that the Lucas factory in Toronto was manufacturing parts for the Orenda engine, fuel systems as a matter of fact, and that they had received capital assistance in the amount of $5,794,000, of which $2,630,000 was for construction and $3,163,000 was for equipment and installations. I wonder if the minister can tell us what other companies as well as this Lucas company have received capital assistance grants so far as the production of the Orenda engine and the CF-100 are concerned, and what that capital assistance was?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should point out that while capital assistance is given to certain plants to make parts for the Orenda engines, these plants also make other defence items. For instance, the Lucas factory makes fuel systems and certain other parts.
The fuel systems are for the Orenda engine?

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No, they are all included in the over-all figure, except for Canadian Steel Improvements. The capital assistance for the Orenda program is put out through A. Y. Roe. This company is charged with the money, and it is passed on by them to their subcontractors.
Then the total amount of capital assistance for the CF-100 and the Orenda would be somewhere between $75 million and $80 million, adding those items to the $63 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The items I have recently given are included in the capital assistance which is given to A. V. Roe and passed on to the subs that they use.
That is included in the figure of $63 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.
So the total capital assistance is $63 million?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

If these moneys are issued by the A.V. Roe Company to the other companies, is the control of that capital assistance in the hands of A. V. Roe or is it in the hands of defence production? Who authorizes that capital assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Title to all the equipment is in the crown. We authorize each item of equipment separately. If the equipment is moved from one of the plants to another, it must be done through permission obtained from the department. Every item of expenditure under the capital assistance fund is registered
4966	HOUSE OF
Supply-Defence Production on the central registry. If there is a transfer, the transfer is made on the central registry and someone is responsible to the crown for delivering back the capital assistance item or payment.
Then if I understand the minister correctly, grants of capital assistance are made by his department on the recommendation of A. V. Roe, in this particular case.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: A. V. Roe would express the need, and it would be vetted by experts from the department. It would have to be approved by the committee of the department which passes on financial problems of this kind, the financial adviser's branch, and then approved by the governor in council.

What check does the minister's department keep on the cost of construction so far as the capital assistance grants are concerned? For example, in connection with this Lucas plant there is $2,630,000 for construction. How does the department control that expenditure, as to whether or not it is properly planned, whether overly expensive construction is being undertaken with that money?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Plans are submitted to the department and they are vetted by the appropriate branch of the department. The expenditure is supervised by Defence Construction Limited.

Does that mean that Defence Construction does actually say to these people, "No; we figure that you are putting in far too expensive a type of floor here"- or whatever it may be-"and you have to cut the cost of this down to 75 per cent of what you are planning"?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Or anything else along that line?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
In connection with this factory, what was the cost per square foot?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I do not know. It is an extremely intricate mechanism that they are making. The factory is air-conditioned. I do not remember the dimensions. I think I could get them quite easily, but not tonight. If this item goes over, I shall try to have them for the hon. member tomorrow.

Perhaps I had better say that I asked some of these questions about this particular factory because I have had two or three letters from people complaining that the type of construction, the cost


of landscaping that was being done, and things of that sort were excessive and that if the dominion government were paying for this, as my correspondents understood they were, they thought there was something wrong in connection with the matter and that the question should be raised. That is why I asked particularly what was the cost per square foot of this factory, so that we might perhaps compare it with the cost of some other factories. If the minister is going to bring in any further information on this matter, I should like to know the cost of what you might call the amenities, particularly in the way of landscaping and things of that sort, in connection with this particular factory.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: While we are on the subject, I might say I am told that the furniture, which is noted by visitors there-I have heard more about the furniture than I have about the building-is rather gaudy; but that is furnished entirely at the expense of the company, as was the landscaping.

I have heard chiefly about the construction of the factory and the landscaping, as it happens, not about the furniture in connection with this matter. I obtained another return on May 6 in connection with the cost of the Canadian Arsenals plant in Toronto. It shows that the total amount of space there was 194,571 square feet and the construction cost-which was, I take it, a government expenditure- was $2,161,000. That worked out at a cost per square foot of $11.1. Another return in connection with the John Inglis Company, a plant which is also in Scarboro, not far away from the Canadian Arsenals plant, shows that this plant had a construction cost of $4,332,000 and that the total space constructed was 186,695 square feet, which works out at a cost per square foot of $23.2. I understand from contractors that $23.2 per square foot is an excessive cost. There may be reasons for that. , I wonder whether the minister could explain why this particular plant should have been such a costly affair?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The reason is quite simple, Mr. Chairman. It is a special plant for extremely large and heavy items of propulsion equipment. There was no existing plant that could manufacture propulsion equipment of that kind, on account of the weight and size of the equipment. It is a high-ceiling building with heavy cranes and, of course, an extremely heavy floor. I might say that all the buildings my hon. friend has mentioned are the property of the crown and will remain the property of the crown. If the contractor did not do his job properly, we paid too much for it.

But if the contractor did a good job, we got value for the money.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Does the minister mean that this Lucas factory is the property of the crown and will remain the property of the crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
Or is that on a repayment basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No.
Mr. Harknessj That remains the property of the crown? '

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.

I wonder whether the minister can tell us the total number of companies -I do not want all the names, the particular amounts and so forth-which have received capital assistance, in addition to the ones he has already given, and the total amount of that capital assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is in the public accounts, schedule B, page DD-20.
That is for the year 1952. But that does not include anything since 1952.
Since March 31, 1952.
Since March 31, 1952 is what I should say.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: At March 31, 1953 the total investment in crown facilities-that is buildings, machinery and any physical equipment furnished under capital assistance- was $233,571,281.78, all the property of the crown.
That would include all this A. V. Roe business in addition to the others, would it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

How many companies are there, all told, or how many does that involve? If the minister has that information I shall be glad to have it; if not, I will not worry about it. How many different properties does that involve?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am told there are 29 in addition to those shown in schedule B.
There are 29 in addition to the ones shown in the public accounts for 1952?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

This is an extremely large item. I wonder whether the minister will indicate to the committee the steps the
Supply-Defence Production department takes with respect to applications for capital assistance? Just what information do they require and what tests do they submit these applications to before expending these sums of money?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The test is whether the item can be produced in Canada from existing facilities. If the department is satisfied that the item cannot be furnished from existing facilities, it then becomes necessary to provide the facilities. They are provided to the firms who seem best equipped to do the work, from the point of view of management and auxiliary facilities. An agreement is reached between the respective firms and the government as to what is needed in the way of both floor space and equipment, and plans are drawn to provide that. The work is carried out under the supervision of Defence Construction Limited for the account of the government. If the hon. member looks at page 14 of the department's annual report, he will find that procedure spelled out there.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall this item carry?
No, Mr. Chairman. I have certain questions about Sorel which I indicated I should like to ask. Perhaps we could call it ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If hon. members are agreeable, perhaps we could finish this item tonight.

I can tell you, Mr. Chairman, that I have another question following up the one I just asked the minister. The information I wanted is not to be found at page 14 of the annual report. Will the minister indicate the financial terms of this capital assistance program as between the government and the companies? Are the terms uniform in all cases or does the department arrange terms to meet the immediate situation of the individual company?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are no terms. All facilities are built for the account of the government, are paid for by the government and are owned by the government, to carry out a government contract. The only case where terms would come in would be if there were not sufficient government work remaining. We have a lease arrangement under which we can lease floor space and machinery for private work, which means a payment to the government. But the facility is owned by the government. It is built on land which is deeded to the government, and it remains the property of the government unless the government at some future date decides to sell it. I may say that of the capital assistance items built during the last war there has been a recovery of about

Supply-Defence Production $650 million. There will be a substantial recovery of the facilities built under the present emergency. I think the recovery was something over 40 per cent of the capital cost.
Will the minister answer this question? Would the general practice be to acquire the freehold-in other words, to hold everything-or would it be to put machinery into already existing premises?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If a plant can carry out a government order simply by the addition of machinery, the machinery is placed in existing buildings; it is stamped with the government number and painted a particular colour. It remains the property of the crown in a privately-owned building. I thought we were discussing a situation where the government had to provide the building as well as the machinery.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Since it is ten o'clock, shall I report progress?
Item stands.
Progress reported.
May we revert to routine proceedings so that I can present a report.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Has the hon. member leave to revert to routine proceedings at this time?
Agreed.
